tool.name: Amazon Web Services
tool.tagline: The largest cloud platform: compute, storage, databases, networking and more
tool.description: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the most widely used cloud platform, offering hundreds of managed services for compute, storage, databases, networking, messaging and security, billed per use. Engineers use it to run everything from single Lambda functions to global, multi-account production systems. Learning its core building blocks, identity model and networking pays off in almost any back-end, data or platform role.

glossary.def: A building full of servers, with its own power, cooling and network connections. Cloud providers run many of them.
A geographic area where AWS runs its own separate group of data centers, such as Frankfurt or N. Virginia, named like eu-central-1.
One or more AWS data centers inside a Region with their own power, cooling and network, so a problem in one zone doesn't take down the others.
A zone name like use1-az1 that means the same physical Availability Zone in every AWS account, unlike names such as us-east-1a, which are shuffled per account.
One of hundreds of small AWS sites in cities worldwide, used to answer users from nearby (for example cached web content) rather than from a faraway Region.
Your own space in AWS: everything you create lives in one account, which is billed separately and walled off from other accounts by default.
The login created with an AWS account (its sign-up email and password). It can do absolutely anything in the account and can't be restricted, so it is locked away.
Multi-factor authentication: logging in needs a second proof besides the password, such as a code from a phone app or a hardware key.
A long-lived ID-and-secret pair that lets a program act as an IAM user in AWS. If it leaks, whoever has it can act as you until it is deleted.
AWS's split of security duties: AWS protects its buildings, hardware and the services it runs; you protect what you set up in them, such as permissions, network rules and your data.
Amazon's command-line program, aws, which turns commands typed in a terminal into requests to AWS services.
A named set of settings for the AWS CLI and SDKs (which account, which permissions, which Region), chosen with --profile or AWS_PROFILE.
The AWS service where people sign in once with their work account and get short-lived access to the AWS accounts and permission sets they've been assigned.
In IAM Identity Center, a named bundle of permissions (such as ReadOnly or Developer) that is given to people for specific AWS accounts.
A small query language for picking and reshaping parts of JSON, used by the AWS CLI's --query option.
AWS credentials that stop working on their own after a set time, usually an hour, so a leaked copy is useful only briefly.
In AWS, whoever makes a request: a person, an IAM user, an IAM role or an AWS service. IAM checks what that principal is allowed to do.
A long-term identity in one AWS account with its own password and/or access keys. Mostly replaced today by IAM roles and IAM Identity Center.
A named collection of IAM users so permissions can be given to all of them at once. A group can't sign in or make requests itself.
An AWS identity with permissions but no password or keys of its own. A person, program or service takes it on (assumes it) and gets temporary credentials.
To take on an IAM role: AWS checks you're allowed to, then hands you temporary credentials that carry the role's permissions.
Amazon Resource Name: the full unique name of an AWS resource, like arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket, used in policies and commands.
A JSON document listing which actions on which AWS resources are allowed or denied, attached to an identity or to a resource.
An IAM policy attached to a user, group or role, saying what that identity may do.
An IAM policy attached to a resource such as an S3 bucket, saying who (which principals) may do what to it.
A resource-based policy attached to an S3 bucket, saying who may do what with the bucket and its objects.
A policy statement with Effect Deny. It always wins: no Allow anywhere can override it.
A reusable IAM policy that can be attached to many identities: written by AWS (AWS managed) or by you (customer managed). An inline policy instead belongs to one identity only.
An AWS tool that checks IAM policies for mistakes, finds resources shared outside your account, and can suggest a tighter policy from what was actually used.
In AWS, rules that block risky actions no matter what other permissions say, usually written as Deny statements or organization-wide policies.
Elastic Compute Cloud: the AWS service that rents you virtual machines (called instances) by the second.
Amazon Machine Image: a saved disk image (operating system plus any installed software) and settings that new EC2 instances are started from.
The size and kind of an EC2 virtual machine, such as m7g.large, which sets its CPUs, memory, network speed and price.
AWS's own ARM-based processors, used in instance types with a g, such as m7g; usually cheaper for the same work if your software runs on ARM64.
A script you hand to an EC2 instance at launch; it runs once as root on first boot, typically to install and start your app.
The wrapper that attaches an IAM role to an EC2 instance, so programs on it get temporary credentials automatically.
A special address only an EC2 instance can reach, which answers questions about the instance and hands out its role's temporary credentials. IMDSv2 is the safer version.
An AWS feature that gives you a shell on an instance through AWS itself, with permissions and logging, so no SSH port or key is needed.
Disks physically inside the host machine of an EC2 instance: very fast, but their data is lost when the instance stops.
Spare EC2 capacity sold at a big discount; AWS can take it back with a two-minute warning, so it suits work that can be interrupted.
The standard way to pay for EC2 and similar compute: by the second or hour, no commitment, at full price.
A way to write a range of IP addresses as a start address and a size, like 10.20.0.0/16. The bigger the number after the slash, the smaller the range.
A smaller slice of a network's address range. In AWS each subnet sits in one Availability Zone and is public or private depending on its routes.
In a VPC, the list of rules that says where network traffic from a subnet goes next, based on the destination address.
The VPC component that connects a VPC to the public internet. Only subnets with a route to it are public.
A managed device that lets servers in private subnets start connections out to the internet while nothing outside can connect in to them.
The ready-made VPC with public subnets that every AWS account gets in each Region; fine for experiments, not for production.
A VPC feature that records which network connections were accepted or rejected, for troubleshooting and security reviews.
A firewall around an AWS resource such as an EC2 instance: it lists which traffic may come in or go out, and blocks everything else.
A simple firewall applied to a whole subnet, with numbered allow and deny rules checked in order; it doesn't remember connections.
A temporary, high-numbered port (roughly 1024-65535) a computer picks for its side of an outgoing connection; replies come back to it.
Elastic network interface: AWS's virtual network card, with a private IP address and security groups, attached to an instance, container or endpoint.
A fixed public IPv4 address you reserve in your account and attach to an instance, NAT gateway or load balancer.
A private doorway from a VPC to an AWS service, so traffic reaches it without going over the internet or through a NAT gateway.
The AWS technology behind interface endpoints: it puts a private address for a service inside your VPC, without connecting the two networks.
A private link between two VPCs so they can talk using private IP addresses; it only connects that one pair.
A regional AWS router that connects many VPCs, accounts and on-premises networks through one central hub.
The AWS service family of managed load balancers: Application, Network and Gateway Load Balancers.
AWS's load balancer for web (HTTP and HTTPS) traffic; it can route requests by things like the URL path or host name.
AWS's load balancer for raw TCP and UDP connections: very fast, with fixed IP addresses, but it doesn't look inside web requests.
The set of servers, containers, IP addresses or functions a load balancer sends traffic to, with a health check that decides which are in service.
On a load balancer, the setting that waits for connections on one protocol and port (such as HTTPS on 443) and decides where they go.
AWS Certificate Manager: issues and renews free TLS certificates for use on load balancers, CloudFront and API Gateway.
AWS's DNS service: it holds the records that turn your domain names into addresses, and can steer users between Regions.
In Route 53, the container for all the DNS records of one domain, such as example.com.
A Route 53 record that points a name straight at an AWS resource (like a load balancer) and follows its changing addresses automatically.
AWS's content delivery network: it keeps copies of your content in edge locations close to users and serves them from there.
In a CDN such as CloudFront, the server or bucket that holds the original content the edge copies come from.
A CloudFront feature that signs requests to a private S3 bucket so only your distribution can read it and the bucket stays private.
Simple Storage Service: AWS's object storage, which keeps files of any size in buckets and serves them over HTTPS.
A named container for files (objects) in S3. Its name is unique across all of AWS and it lives in one Region.
The full name of a file in an S3 bucket, such as reports/2026/q3.csv. The slashes are just characters; there are no real folders.
An S3 price tier for objects: cheaper classes cost less to store but more, or take longer, to read back.
A rule that automatically moves S3 objects (or images) to a cheaper tier or deletes them after a set age.
An S3 bucket setting that keeps every old version of an object when it is overwritten or deleted, so mistakes can be undone.
How unlikely it is that stored data is ever lost. S3 aims for 99.999999999%, by keeping copies in several places.
Uploading a big file to S3 in many parts, possibly at once, and joining them at the end; a failed part is retried alone.
A temporary web link, signed with someone's AWS credentials, that lets whoever holds it read or upload one S3 object until it expires.
S3 settings, on by default, that stop a bucket or account from ever being made public by a policy or permission mistake.
Encryption that an AWS service applies to your data when it stores it, and removes when an allowed caller reads it. SSE-KMS uses a KMS key you control.
Elastic Block Store: network disks for EC2 instances. A volume lives in one Availability Zone and keeps its data when the instance stops.
Elastic File System: a shared network file system that many instances and containers in different Availability Zones can mount at once.
SSD: a solid-state drive, storage on chips with no moving parts, fast at jumping around. An HDD is a spinning hard disk: cheaper, good at long sequential reads.
Input/output operations per second: how many separate reads or writes a disk can do each second. Databases care a lot about it.
Network File System: a standard way for computers to mount and use a folder that lives on another machine over the network.
Relational Database Service: AWS runs a database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL for you, handling setup, updates, backups and failover.
The database software itself, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, that stores the data and answers SQL queries.
In RDS, the size of the server running the database (CPUs and memory), named like db.m7g.large.
An RDS setting that keeps an up-to-date standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone and switches to it automatically if the main one fails.
A spare copy of a database kept up to date and ready to take over if the main one fails.
Restoring a database to how it was at any chosen second within the backup retention period.
A managed go-between for RDS that keeps a small pool of open database connections and shares them among many short-lived clients.
AWS's own MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible database with a shared storage layer kept in three Availability Zones, fast failover and up to 15 readers.
AWS's serverless key-value database: no servers to manage, you create a table and read or write items through an API, in milliseconds at any scale.
In DynamoDB, one record in a table, a set of named attributes, found by its primary key; like a row in other databases.
The optional second part of a DynamoDB primary key; items with the same partition key are stored together, ordered by it.
A secondary index in DynamoDB: an extra copy of chosen attributes, keyed differently, so you can query the table by something other than its main key.
One partition key getting far more traffic than the rest, so it hits per-partition limits and gets throttled while others sit idle.
Preventing lost updates by saving only if a version number is still what you read; if someone else saved in between, your write fails and you retry.
A time-ordered log of every change to a DynamoDB table that Lambda can read to react to inserts, updates and deletes.
AWS Lambda: a service that runs a piece of your code (a function) only when something triggers it; you pay for the milliseconds it runs and never manage a server.
The function in your Lambda code that AWS calls for each event, such as def handler(event, context).
The IAM role a Lambda function runs as; it decides which AWS actions the function's code may perform.
The small, isolated sandbox Lambda starts to run one copy of your function; it is reused for later calls while it stays warm.
A Lambda setting that makes Lambda itself read messages from a queue or stream and call your function with them in batches.
A built-in HTTPS address for a single Lambda function, so it can be called from the web without API Gateway.
Lambda settings for how many copies may run at once: reserved concurrency guarantees and caps a function's share; provisioned concurrency keeps copies warmed up in advance.
AWS's managed front door for web APIs: it receives HTTPS requests, checks and limits them, and passes them to Lambda or other back ends.
An API Gateway check that runs before your code to decide whether a request is allowed, for example by validating a login token.
Simple Queue Service: AWS's managed message queue, which holds messages until a consumer fetches and deletes them.
Simple Notification Service: publish a message once to a topic and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber (queues, functions, email, SMS).
In SQS, how long a received message stays hidden from other consumers; if it isn't deleted in that time, it reappears for another try.
A side queue where messages go after failing too many times, so they can be inspected later instead of blocking or looping forever.
Sending one message to many receivers at once, such as one SNS topic delivering a copy to several queues.
AWS's event router: services and apps send JSON events to an event bus, and rules forward matching events to targets such as Lambda or SQS.
In EventBridge, a JSON description of which events a rule should match, by fields like source and detail.
Elastic Container Registry: AWS's private registry for storing container images.
Elastic Container Service: AWS's own system for running and keeping containers running, scaled and connected to load balancers.
A way to run ECS (or EKS) containers where AWS provides the machines: you pay per container's CPU and memory and never manage servers.
In ECS, the versioned JSON blueprint for running containers: images, CPU and memory, ports, settings, logs and IAM roles.
In ECS, one running copy of a task definition: one or more containers started together.
In ECS, the setting that keeps a chosen number of tasks running, replaces failed ones and connects them to a load balancer.
In ECS, the task role is the IAM role your containers' code uses; the task execution role is the one ECS itself uses to pull images and write logs.
Elastic Kubernetes Service: AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you, and you choose how the worker machines are provided.
A widely used open-source system for running containers across many machines, keeping the desired number running and connected.
In Kubernetes, the smallest unit it runs: one or more containers scheduled together on one machine and sharing a network address.
In Kubernetes, one machine (here, usually an EC2 instance) that runs pods.
AWS's monitoring service: it collects metrics and logs from your resources and can raise alarms.
A watch on one CloudWatch metric that switches to ALARM when a threshold is crossed and can notify people or trigger an action.
In CloudWatch Logs, a log group holds the logs of one application; each source (such as one container) writes its own log stream inside it.
A CloudWatch tool for searching and summarising log groups with a short query language.
A CloudWatch Logs rule that counts log lines matching a pattern and turns the count into a metric you can alarm on.
AWS's audit log: it records the API calls made in your account, by whom, when and from where.

CloudTrail categories: management events are changes to resources (create, delete, configure) and are logged by default; data events are high-volume reads and writes of data, logged only if you enable them.
An AWS service that records how each resource's settings change over time and checks them against rules.
An AWS service that watches account activity and network logs for signs of attack, such as stolen credentials in use.
A tag key (like team) you activate in AWS billing so costs can be split by its values in reports.
An AWS billing tool that emails or alerts you when actual or forecast spending passes an amount you set.
The AWS billing tool for charts and breakdowns of what you spent, by service, account, Region or tag.
AWS's free allowances for new and existing accounts, such as a million Lambda requests per month.
AWS's infrastructure-as-code service: you describe resources in a YAML or JSON template and it creates, updates and deletes them for you as a stack.
In CloudFormation (and CDK), one deployed copy of a template: the group of resources it created and manages together.
A CloudFormation preview of exactly what an update will add, change, replace or delete, which you review before running it.
The name a resource has inside a CloudFormation template; CloudFormation uses it to track which real resource belongs to which entry.
AWS Cloud Development Kit: write infrastructure as ordinary code (Python, TypeScript and others) that is turned into CloudFormation templates.
In CDK, a building block class representing one or more AWS resources; you combine constructs inside stacks.
AWS discounts in return for committing to a steady amount of compute spending (Savings Plans) or specific resources (Reserved Instances) for one or three years.
Switching a resource to a smaller (or larger) size that matches what it actually uses, so you stop paying for idle capacity.
An EC2 feature that keeps a fleet of identical instances between a minimum and maximum size, replacing failed ones and adding or removing instances as load changes.
A saved, versioned recipe for starting EC2 instances: AMI, instance type, security groups, IAM role, user data and so on.
Key Management Service: AWS's vault for encryption keys. Keys never leave it; you ask KMS to encrypt or decrypt, and every use is logged.
Encrypting data with a fresh data key, then encrypting that small data key with a master key kept in KMS, and storing the two together.
A one-off encryption key, generated by KMS, that you use to encrypt actual data locally; you store only its encrypted copy.
The resource-based policy on a KMS key; it decides who may use or manage the key, and IAM policies count only if it allows them to.
Non-secret key-value pairs bound to KMS-encrypted data; decryption fails unless the same pairs are supplied again, and they appear in audit logs.
AWS's secrets manager: it stores passwords and API keys encrypted, versions them and can rotate some (like database passwords) automatically.
A simple AWS store for configuration values and secrets (SecureString), cheaper than Secrets Manager but without automatic rotation.
Security Token Service: the AWS service that hands out temporary credentials when someone assumes an IAM role.
The resource-based policy on an IAM role that says who is allowed to assume it.
The third part of temporary AWS credentials, sent with the access key ID and secret; it proves the credentials came from STS and when they expire.
The official AWS SDK for Python: a library that turns Python method calls into requests to AWS services.
The ordered list of places the AWS CLI and SDKs look for credentials: environment variables, config files and profiles, then the role of the container or instance they run on.
A boto3 helper that keeps calling a list operation page after page until every result has been returned.
A boto3 or CLI helper that repeatedly checks a resource until it reaches a state, such as an instance running.
The AWS service for managing many AWS accounts together: grouping them, paying with one bill and applying organization-wide policies.
The AWS account that creates an organization, pays its bill and manages it; it should run no workloads.
A folder of AWS accounts inside an organization, such as Prod or Sandbox; policies attached to it apply to every account inside.
Organization-wide policies that set the maximum permissions in member accounts: SCPs cap what principals can do, RCPs cap what can be done to resources. They never grant anything.
A prepared multi-account AWS setup with shared logging, security accounts, guardrails and a way to create new accounts, often built with AWS Control Tower.
A policy set on an IAM user or role that caps the most its identity policies can ever grant, whatever they say.
A security problem where a trusted service is tricked into using its access on behalf of someone who shouldn't have it.
The control plane is the part of a service that creates, changes and deletes things; the data plane is the part that does the everyday work, like serving reads and writes.
A system is eventually consistent when a change may take a moment to show up everywhere; strongly consistent means every read sees the latest write at once.
Recovery point objective: how much recent data, measured in time, you can afford to lose in a disaster.
Recovery time objective: how long a system may be down before it must be working again after a disaster.
Designing so a system keeps working through a failure with what is already running, without having to create or change anything during the incident.
When two copies of a system each think they are the main one and both accept changes, so their data drifts apart.
AWS's checklist of design questions grouped into six pillars (operations, security, reliability, performance, cost, sustainability) for reviewing a system.
A random amount added to a wait time, so many clients that failed together don't all retry at the same moment.
AWS's per-account limits on how many resources you may have or how fast you may call an API, some raisable on request.
A unique value you send with a create request; if you retry with the same value, AWS returns the first result instead of creating a duplicate.

concepts.name: Regions, Availability Zones and edge
concepts.summary: AWS runs in separate Regions around the world, each made of several Availability Zones, plus small edge locations close to users.
concepts.why: Where you put something decides how fast it is for users, what one failure can take down, what it costs and which country's laws apply to its data.
concepts.body:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) rents out computing over the internet. Instead of buying servers, you ask AWS for what you need (a virtual machine, space for files, a database) and pay only for what you use. Each kind of offering is a **service**, and AWS has hundreds of them.

All of it runs in AWS's **data centers**: large buildings full of servers, with their own power and cooling. AWS groups them by geography into **Regions**, such as `us-east-1` (N. Virginia) or `eu-central-1` (Frankfurt). Each Region is run separately from the others, and your data stays in the Region you chose unless you copy it out.

Inside a Region there are three or more **Availability Zones** (AZs). An AZ is one or more data centers with their own power, cooling and network, a few kilometres from the others and joined to them by fast private cables. If one AZ loses power, the others keep going. That is why systems that must stay up, which engineers call **high availability**, run copies in at least two AZs.

Every service works at one of three levels, and knowing which saves confusion:

- **Global**: the same everywhere, such as the list of people and permissions in your account.
- **Regional**: most services, such as file storage; you pick a Region when you create something.
- **Zonal**: tied to one AZ, such as a single virtual machine and its disk.

**Edge locations** are hundreds of small AWS sites in cities worldwide. They answer users from nearby, which cuts **latency**: the delay before data arrives.

AZ names such as `us-east-1a` are shuffled per account, so your `1a` may be a different building from a colleague's `1a` in another account. When two accounts must agree on a zone, use the **AZ ID**, such as `use1-az1`, which is the same everywhere.

Choose a Region by distance to your users, laws about where data may be stored, which services it offers, and price, which differs between Regions.
concepts.code:
# These use the AWS command-line tool, set up in a later lesson.
# List the Regions this account can use
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output text
# eu-central-1  us-east-1  us-west-2 ...

# Zone names next to their stable AZ IDs in one Region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region eu-central-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId]' --output text
# eu-central-1a  euc1-az2
# eu-central-1b  euc1-az3
# eu-central-1c  euc1-az1
takeaways: Region = a separate geographic area; AZ = an independent group of data centers inside it
Services are global, regional or zonal; check which before designing
Run copies in two or more AZs to survive a data-center failure
Use AZ IDs, not names, when matching zones across accounts
pitfalls: Assuming us-east-1a is the same physical zone in every account.

quiz.q: Which of these is tied to a single Availability Zone?
options: Your account's list of users and permissions
A single virtual machine and its disk
quiz.explain: A virtual machine and its disk live in one AZ; storage is regional and user permissions are global.

quiz.q: Why does running in two Availability Zones help a system survive a data-center outage?
options: AZs have separate power, cooling and networking, so one can fail while the other runs
AZs share power but have separate networks
AWS automatically moves your machines between AZs
Each AZ is in a different Region
quiz.explain: AZs are built as independent failure areas within a Region; AWS does not move your machines for you.

concepts.name: Accounts, root user and shared responsibility
concepts.summary: An AWS account is your walled-off, separately billed space; lock away its all-powerful root user and know what AWS secures versus what you do.
concepts.why: Most serious AWS break-ins start with a leaked password or key, or with a misunderstanding of who is responsible for what.
concepts.body:
Everything you create in AWS lives inside an **AWS account**. The account is the unit of billing and the main security wall: by default nothing in one account can touch another. It also has **quotas**, limits such as how many virtual machines it may run at once. Larger companies use many accounts, one per team or environment; a later lesson covers that.

Signing up creates the **root user**: the sign-up email and password. Root can do anything at all in the account, and none of the usual permission settings can limit it. Treat it like the spare key to a building, kept in a safe:

- Turn on **MFA** (multi-factor authentication): logging in then also needs a code from your phone or a hardware key. AWS now requires it.
- Never create an **access key** for root. An access key is a long-lived ID and secret that lets a program act as you; if it leaks, anyone can use it.
- Use root only for the few jobs that need it, such as closing the account.
- Do daily work with personal logins that have only the permissions you need (the identity lessons show how).

Those logins and permissions are managed by **IAM** (identity and access management), the AWS service that decides who may do what. The proof of who you are, such as a password or key, is called your **credentials**.

The **shared responsibility model** splits security work. AWS protects the cloud itself: buildings, hardware and the software that runs its services. You protect what you put in it: who has access, network rules, your data, and whether it is **encrypted** (scrambled so only key holders can read it).

The line moves with the service:

- On **EC2**, where you rent a whole virtual machine, you install the operating system's security updates.
- On **RDS**, where AWS runs a **database** for you (an organised store of data that programs can search and update quickly), AWS updates the database software, but you still decide who may connect.
- On **Lambda**, which runs just a piece of your code when needed, AWS handles everything except your code and its permissions.

A misconfiguration, such as a file store left public, is always on your side of the line.
concepts.code:
# Who am I, and in which account?
aws sts get-caller-identity
# { "UserId": "AROA...:alice", "Account": "111122223333", ... }

# Does root have MFA, and does it have any access keys?
aws iam get-account-summary \
  --query 'SummaryMap.[AccountMFAEnabled,AccountAccessKeysPresent]'
# [1, 0]   -> root has MFA, root has no access keys (what you want)
takeaways: The account is the security and billing boundary
Root: MFA on, no access keys, used only for the few jobs that need it
AWS secures the hardware and services; you secure settings, access and data
pitfalls: Doing everyday work as root or with a long-lived access key.

quiz.q: You rent a virtual machine on EC2. Who installs security updates for its operating system?
options: AWS, because it owns the hardware
AWS Support, if you pay for it
quiz.explain: On EC2 you manage the operating system; AWS manages the physical machines underneath.

quiz.q: What is the recommended use of the root user?
options: Only the few tasks that need root, protected by MFA
Running the command-line tool on laptops
quiz.explain: Root can't be restricted, so it is kept for root-only tasks and protected with MFA.

concepts.name: The AWS CLI: profiles, SSO and --query
concepts.summary: Install the AWS CLI, sign in through IAM Identity Center with named profiles, and pick out just the data you need with --query.
concepts.why: The command line is the fastest way to look around AWS and to script it, and the same sign-in setup is reused by every programming library for AWS.
concepts.body:
Everything in AWS is done by sending requests to an **API**: a fixed menu of operations a service offers to programs, such as "start a virtual machine" or "list my files". Each call is a **request** sent over the internet, and AWS sends back a **response**, usually as JSON. The website (the AWS console) and every tool are just friendly ways of sending those requests.

The **AWS CLI** is Amazon's command-line program, `aws`. Each API operation becomes a command: `aws <service> <operation> --option value`. Add `help` to any command, such as `aws s3api put-object help`, to read its manual. Programming libraries for AWS, called **SDKs**, offer the same operations to code.

Settings and credentials live in `~/.aws/config` and `~/.aws/credentials`, grouped into **profiles**: named sets of settings, one per account or job. Choose one with `--profile dev` or `export AWS_PROFILE=dev`, and a Region with `--region` or `AWS_REGION`.

The recommended way to sign in is **IAM Identity Center**, where you log in once with your work account. `aws configure sso` writes a profile for it. Then `aws sso login` opens your web **browser** to log in, and the CLI saves **temporary credentials** that expire after a few hours.

The older `aws configure` asks for an access key instead and stores that long-lived **secret** on disk, which you should avoid.

Output can be `json` (the default), `yaml`, `text` or `table`. Two options look alike but work differently:

- `--filters` is sent to AWS, so the service returns fewer results.
- `--query` is applied by the CLI to the response it got. It uses **JMESPath**, a small language for picking parts of JSON.

Long lists come back in pages, and the CLI fetches every page for you; `--max-items` limits how many you get. In scripts, set `AWS_PAGER=""` so output isn't sent to a pager like `less`.

S3, AWS's file storage, has handy extra commands (`aws s3 cp`, `aws s3 sync`, `aws s3 ls`) next to the raw API ones in `aws s3api`. Many EC2 commands that change things accept `--dry-run`, which only checks that you'd be allowed.
concepts.code:
# ~/.aws/config written by `aws configure sso`
# [profile dev]
# sso_session = acme
# sso_account_id = 111122223333
# sso_role_name = DeveloperAccess
# region = eu-west-1
# [sso-session acme]
# sso_start_url = https://acme.awsapps.com/start
# sso_region = eu-west-1

aws sso login --profile dev
export AWS_PROFILE=dev AWS_PAGER=""

# Filter on the AWS side, then pick two fields from each result
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType]' --output table

aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[?starts_with(Name, `logs-`)].Name' --output text
# logs-prod  logs-staging
takeaways: Every AWS action is an API request; the CLI and SDKs send them for you
Use profiles and IAM Identity Center (aws sso login) instead of stored access keys
--filters runs at AWS; --query (JMESPath) runs in the CLI on the response
aws s3 has convenience commands; aws s3api is the raw API
pitfalls: Saving a long-lived access key in ~/.aws/credentials on a laptop or a build server.

quiz.q: You need only the IDs of running virtual machines. Which combination is most efficient?
options: --filters to select running machines at AWS, --query to pick out the IDs
quiz.explain: --filters makes AWS return less; --query then picks the fields you want from the response.

quiz.q: Which command signs a profile in through IAM Identity Center?
quiz.explain: aws sso login opens the browser sign-in and saves temporary credentials for that profile.

concepts.name: IAM: users, groups, roles and principals
concepts.summary: IAM decides who may call which AWS action: every request comes from a principal and is refused unless a policy allows it.
concepts.why: Every action in AWS, from a click in the console to code running in Lambda, is a request that IAM checks, so everything else builds on it.
concepts.body:
Every request to AWS comes from someone or something: a person, a script, a service. AWS calls that caller a **principal**. For each request IAM asks two questions. First, who is this? Checking that is **authentication**, like showing ID at a door. Second, may they do this? Checking that is **authorization**.

The answer is "no" unless a permission document, an **IAM policy**, says yes. IAM itself is global (the same in every Region) and free.

The kinds of identity:

- **IAM users**: a long-term login for one person or program, with a password and/or access keys. Today they are for exceptions only, such as an outside tool that can't use roles.
- **IAM groups**: a set of users, so permissions can be given to all of them at once. A group can't sign in or make requests itself.
- **IAM roles**: an identity with permissions but no password or keys of its own. Someone allowed to **assume the role** gets temporary credentials that carry its permissions.
- **Federated users**: people who log in with their company account (through IAM Identity Center) and end up using a role.

Roles are how almost everything gets access. A virtual machine, a Lambda function, an automated build-and-deploy pipeline, or a colleague from another AWS account all assume roles. Nothing long-lived exists that could leak.

The modern pattern: people sign in through IAM Identity Center; programs running on AWS use roles; IAM users with access keys are rare and reviewed.

Every resource has a full name, an **ARN** (Amazon Resource Name): `arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource`. For example, `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/orders-fn` names a role; IAM is global, so the Region part is empty.

The guiding rule is **least privilege**: give each principal only the actions and resources it needs. Start narrow and widen when there's a real need. AWS's ready-made policies, like `ReadOnlyAccess`, are handy starting points but usually allow more than necessary.
concepts.code:
# A group for auditors, using a ready-made AWS policy
aws iam create-group --group-name auditors
aws iam attach-group-policy --group-name auditors \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/SecurityAudit

aws iam create-user --user-name legacy-scanner
aws iam add-user-to-group --group-name auditors --user-name legacy-scanner

aws iam list-attached-group-policies --group-name auditors \
  --query 'AttachedPolicies[].PolicyName' --output text
# SecurityAudit

# Full names (ARNs) of roles whose names start with "orders"
aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[?starts_with(RoleName, `orders`)].Arn'
takeaways: Everything is denied unless a policy allows it
Roles hand out temporary credentials and are the default for programs and people
Groups organise users but can't make requests themselves
ARNs are the full names of resources, used in policies
pitfalls: Creating an IAM user with access keys for a program running on AWS, instead of giving it a role.

quiz.q: A Lambda function needs to write to a database table. What should give it credentials?
options: An IAM user's access keys stored in its settings
An IAM role that the Lambda service assumes for it
quiz.explain: Programs on AWS use roles; the service assumes the role and receives temporary credentials that renew automatically.

quiz.q: Which of these can make requests to AWS as a principal?
quiz.explain: Users, roles and AWS services are principals; groups only collect users, and policies and ARNs are documents and names.

concepts.name: Writing IAM policies
concepts.summary: Read and write JSON policies (Effect, Action, Resource, Condition), tell identity policies from resource policies, and see why a Deny always wins.
concepts.why: Least privilege is only as good as the policies you write, and most "access denied" puzzles turn out to be policy mistakes.
concepts.body:
A policy is a JSON document. It has a `Version` (always `"2012-10-17"`) and a list of **statements**, each one a rule. A statement has:

- `Effect`: `Allow` or `Deny`.
- `Action`: which API operations, like `s3:GetObject` (read a file from S3). Wildcards work: `s3:Get*`.
- `Resource`: the ARNs the actions apply to.
- `Condition` (optional): extra tests on the request, such as where it comes from (`aws:SourceIp`), which Region it targets (`aws:RequestedRegion`), or a tag on the caller (`aws:PrincipalTag/team`).

The examples here use **S3**, AWS's file storage service, which keeps files (called objects) in named containers called **buckets**.

There are two places a policy can live:

- An **identity-based policy** is attached to a user, group or role and says what *that identity* may do. It has no `Principal` field, because the identity is implied.
- A **resource-based policy** is attached to a resource, such as an S3 **bucket policy**, and says *who* may do what to it. It must name a `Principal`.

Identity policies come in three kinds: written by AWS (AWS managed), written by you and reusable (customer managed), or embedded in one identity only (inline). Prefer customer managed for your own.

How a request is decided: everything starts denied. A matching `Allow` permits it. But an **explicit deny**, a matching `Deny` in any policy, beats every Allow. That makes Deny statements good **guardrails**: rules that block a risky action no matter what else is allowed.

A classic gotcha is the resource name. In S3, listing a bucket (`s3:ListBucket`) applies to the bucket itself, `arn:aws:s3:::bucket`. Reading a file (`s3:GetObject`) applies to the files inside, `arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*`. Use the wrong one and you get AccessDenied even though the action is right.

Write policies narrow, then let **IAM Access Analyzer** check them. It can also suggest a tighter policy based on the actions a role actually used.
takeaways: Statement = Effect + Action + Resource (+ Condition)
Resource policies name a Principal; identity policies don't
Default deny, Allow grants, an explicit Deny always wins
S3 bucket-level and file-level actions need different ARNs
pitfalls: Granting s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket (no /*), which matches no files.

quiz.q: A role has a policy allowing s3:* on a bucket and another policy denying s3:DeleteObject on it. Can it delete files?
options: No, an explicit deny overrides any allow
It depends on which policy was attached first
quiz.explain: An explicit Deny always takes precedence over Allows, whatever the order.

quiz.q: Which policy must contain a Principal element?
options: An inline policy on a role
A policy attached to a group
quiz.explain: Resource-based policies such as bucket policies must say who they apply to, using Principal.

concepts.name: EC2 instances, AMIs and instance types
concepts.summary: Rent virtual machines on EC2: start them from AMIs, choose an instance type, set them up with user data, and connect without opening SSH.
concepts.why: EC2 is the base many other AWS services run on, and knowing its settings explains most of how AWS compute behaves and is priced.
concepts.body:
**EC2** (Elastic Compute Cloud) rents you virtual machines by the second. Each running machine is called an **instance**. You start an instance from an **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image): a saved disk image with an operating system and any installed software, much like a Docker image but for a whole machine. The instance runs in one Availability Zone, inside your private network in AWS (a **VPC**, covered next).

An **instance type** sets the machine's size: its CPUs, memory, network speed and price. Names read like `m7g.large`:

- The family letter: `m` general purpose, `c` extra CPU, `r` extra memory, `t` cheap machines for mostly idle work, `g` and `p` with graphics chips (**GPUs**) for AI and graphics.
- The generation: `7`. Newer is usually faster and cheaper.
- The processor: `g` means **Graviton**, AWS's own ARM processors, usually the best value if your software runs on ARM; `i` is Intel and `a` is AMD.
- The size: `large`, `xlarge`, `2xlarge` and so on.

Settings you will set at every launch:

- A **security group**: a **firewall**, meaning a list of rules saying which network traffic may reach the machine.
- The subnet: which part of your network it joins, which decides whether the internet can reach it.
- An **instance profile**: it attaches an IAM role, so programs on the machine get temporary credentials without any stored keys.
- **User data**: a script that runs as root the first time the machine starts up (**boots**), usually to install and start your app.
- Require IMDSv2 (`HttpTokens=required`). The **instance metadata service** is a special address only the machine itself can reach; it hands out the role's credentials, and version 2 blocks common tricks for stealing them.

Connect with **Session Manager** instead of SSH. It gives you a shell through AWS itself, so no port 22 is open, no SSH keys exist, and every session is logged. It needs the SSM agent (preinstalled on Amazon Linux) and the `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` policy on the role.

*Stopping* an instance pauses it: you stop paying for the machine but keep its main disk, an **EBS** volume (a network disk; see the storage lessons). *Terminating* deletes the instance and, by default, that disk. Some types also have **instance store** disks inside the host: fast, but wiped when the machine stops. A public IPv4 address costs extra per hour, so avoid one where you can.

Treat instances as replaceable: script their setup instead of configuring a server by hand.
concepts.code:
# Look up the newest Amazon Linux image for ARM machines (AWS publishes its ID)
AMI=$(aws ssm get-parameter \
  --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64 \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text)

ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI" --instance-type t4g.small \
  --subnet-id subnet-0a1b2c3d --security-group-ids sg-0a1b2c3d \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=ssm-core \
  --metadata-options HttpTokens=required \
  --user-data file://init.sh \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=web-1}]' \
  --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)

aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids "$ID"
aws ssm start-session --target "$ID"        # a shell, no SSH port needed

aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids "$ID"       # keeps the EBS disk
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids "$ID"  # gone for good
takeaways: Instance = AMI + instance type + subnet + security groups + IAM role + user data
Read type names: family, generation, processor, size
Use Session Manager instead of SSH keys and open ports
Stop keeps the EBS disk; terminate and instance store lose data
pitfalls: Keeping important data on instance store disks, or hand-configuring a server nobody can rebuild.

quiz.q: What does the g in m7g.large tell you?
options: It uses an AWS Graviton (ARM) processor
quiz.explain: The letter after the generation number names the processor; g means Graviton.

quiz.q: You stop (not terminate) an instance whose disk is an EBS volume. What do you keep paying for?
quiz.explain: Machine billing stops, but the EBS volume still exists and is billed.

concepts.name: VPCs, subnets and route tables
concepts.summary: A VPC is your private network in a Region: split its address range into subnets in each AZ, and use route tables to make them public or private.
concepts.why: Most servers, databases and containers in AWS live inside a VPC, and network mistakes are the most common reason something "can't connect".
concepts.body:
Computers on a network find each other by **IP addresses**: numbers like `10.20.3.17`, a bit like street addresses. An address has four parts, each from 0 to 255.

A **VPC** (virtual private cloud) is your own private network inside one AWS Region. Nothing can reach it unless you connect it. When you create one, you give it a range of addresses written as a **CIDR block**, such as `10.20.0.0/16`. The number after the slash says how much of the address is fixed. `/16` fixes the first two parts, so it covers every address starting `10.20.` (65,536 of them); `/24` fixes three parts (256 addresses). Each step up halves the range, so a bigger number means a smaller range. A VPC can be from `/16` to `/28`.

Pick ranges that don't overlap with your other VPCs or office networks: overlapping networks can't be joined together later.

A **subnet** is a slice of the VPC's range that lives in exactly **one** Availability Zone. AWS keeps five addresses in every subnet for its own use (such as the VPC's router), so a `/24` subnet leaves 251 for you. Create subnets in at least two AZs.

Traffic leaving a subnet is directed by its **route table**: a list of rules of the form "addresses in this range: send them there". The most specific matching rule wins. Every route table has a `local` rule for the whole VPC range, so all subnets in a VPC can reach each other.

What makes a subnet public or private is only its routes:

- **Public subnet**: a rule sends `0.0.0.0/0` (any address, so the internet) to an **internet gateway**, the VPC's door to the internet. Servers there also need a public IP address to be reachable.
- **Private subnet**: no route to the internet gateway, so nothing on the internet can reach its servers. To download updates they go out through a **NAT gateway**, which allows outgoing connections only (a later lesson).

The usual layout spans two or three AZs: public subnets for **load balancers** (machines that spread incoming traffic across several servers), private subnets for application servers, and subnets with no internet access at all for databases.

Every account has a **default VPC** in each Region with public subnets: handy for experiments, not for real systems. When something can't connect, turn on **VPC Flow Logs**, which record which connections were let through or blocked.
concepts.code:
VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)

PUB=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC" --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/24 \
  --availability-zone eu-west-1a --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
PRIV=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC" --cidr-block 10.20.10.0/24 \
  --availability-zone eu-west-1a --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)

IGW=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id "$VPC" --internet-gateway-id "$IGW"

# A route table that sends internet traffic to the gateway makes a subnet public
RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id "$VPC" --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id "$RT" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "$IGW"
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id "$RT" --subnet-id "$PUB"

aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids "$PUB" --query 'Subnets[0].AvailableIpAddressCount'
# 251
takeaways: A subnet lives in exactly one AZ; AWS keeps 5 addresses in each
Public vs private is decided by the route table: a route to an internet gateway or not
Choose non-overlapping address ranges up front
Spread each layer across at least two AZs
pitfalls: Picking a tiny or overlapping VPC range, which can't be fixed without rebuilding.

quiz.q: What makes a subnet 'public'?
options: A route table rule sending 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway
Its address range being a public one
quiz.explain: Public is purely about having a route to an internet gateway (plus servers having public IP addresses).

quiz.q: How many usable IPv4 addresses does a /28 subnet have in AWS?
quiz.explain: A /28 has 16 addresses and AWS keeps 5, leaving 11.

concepts.name: Security groups and network ACLs
concepts.summary: Security groups are firewalls on each resource that remember connections; network ACLs are simpler rules on whole subnets that don't.
concepts.why: Correct firewall rules are the difference between a private database and a break-in, and the first thing to check when traffic fails.
concepts.body:
Network traffic travels as **packets**: small chunks of data, each labelled with where it comes from and where it goes. The label includes a port, the number that picks which program on a machine receives it: 22 for SSH, 443 for secure websites (**HTTPS**), 5432 for a PostgreSQL database. Most traffic uses **TCP**, the internet's standard way of delivering data reliably and in order.

A security group (SG) is a firewall attached to a resource's **network interface**, its virtual network card. EC2 instances, load balancers, databases and containers in a VPC all have one. How it behaves:

- **Allow rules only**. Anything not allowed is blocked.
- **Stateful**: it remembers connections. If a request is allowed in, the reply is allowed out automatically, and the other way round.
- A new SG allows all outgoing traffic and no incoming traffic.
- A rule's source can be an address range or **another security group**. That is the usual way to build layers: the database SG allows port 5432 *from the app servers' SG*. Any app server can connect, whatever its IP address, and nothing else can.

Rule changes take effect immediately, and one network interface can have several SGs, whose rules add up.

**Network ACLs** (NACLs) sit at the edge of a subnet and apply to everything in it. They are **stateless**: they don't remember connections and judge each packet on its own. Their rules are numbered, checked in order, and can say Deny.

Because NACLs are stateless, you must allow the replies yourself. Replies go back to an **ephemeral port**: a temporary port number, between 1024 and 65535, that the other side picked for its end of the connection. The default NACL allows everything, and most teams leave it so, using SGs for the real control.

When something can't connect, check in this order: route tables, the target's SG (incoming), the source's SG (outgoing), NACLs both ways, then the machine's own firewall and whether the program is listening. VPC Reachability Analyzer can do much of this for you.

Never allow `0.0.0.0/0` (the whole internet) in to SSH, Windows remote desktop (RDP) or database ports.
concepts.code:
WEB=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name web-alb --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d \
  --description "Public HTTPS" --query GroupId --output text)
APP=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name app --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d \
  --description "App tier" --query GroupId --output text)

# Internet -> load balancer on 443 (HTTPS)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id "$WEB" \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# Load balancer's SG -> app servers on 8080 (no IP addresses involved)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id "$APP" \
  --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group "$WEB"

aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules --filters Name=group-id,Values="$APP" \
  --query 'SecurityGroupRules[?!IsEgress].[FromPort,ReferencedGroupInfo.GroupId]' --output text
# 8080  sg-0web...
takeaways: Security groups: allow-only, stateful, attached to network interfaces
Use another security group as the source to build layers
NACLs: stateless, ordered, can deny, apply to whole subnets
When traffic fails, check routes, SGs, NACLs, then the machine itself
pitfalls: Adding a NACL rule for incoming traffic but forgetting to allow the replies out on the ephemeral ports.

quiz.q: An instance's SG allows incoming TCP 443 and has no outgoing rules at all. Can clients get HTTPS replies?
options: No, an outgoing rule must allow the reply
Only if the NACL allows it and the SG has an outgoing rule
quiz.explain: SGs remember connections, so replies to allowed incoming traffic are always let out.

quiz.q: What is the best way to let only the app servers reach the database on port 5432?
options: Use a NACL deny for everything else
Allow 5432 from the whole VPC range
Allow 5432 from the app servers' security group
quiz.explain: Using the app SG as the source admits exactly the app servers, whatever their IP addresses.

concepts.name: S3: buckets, objects and storage classes
concepts.summary: Store any amount of data as objects in S3 buckets, pick a storage class by how often it's read, and let lifecycle rules move or delete old data.
concepts.why: S3 is where almost everything gets stored on AWS: website files, backups (spare copies to restore from), logs, data for analysis and the output of builds.
concepts.body:
**S3** (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's storage for files of any kind. It calls each file an **object**: the file's bytes plus **metadata**, small labels about it such as its content type. Objects live in **buckets**, named containers, and each object is found by its **key**, its full name inside the bucket. One object can be up to 5 TB (5 **terabytes**, about 5,000 gigabytes).

Bucket names are unique across all of AWS, but each bucket lives in one Region, and the data stays there unless you set up **replication** (automatic copying) to another bucket. S3 is built for extreme **durability**, meaning data is almost never lost: it aims for 99.999999999% by keeping copies in several AZs.

There are no real folders. `reports/2026/q3.csv` is one key, and the console simply groups keys by their `/` prefixes. S3 is also strongly consistent: as soon as an upload succeeds, every read and every listing sees it.

Each object has a **storage class**, a price tier. Cheaper tiers cost less per gigabyte stored but charge more, or take longer, to read back:

- **Standard** for data read often.
- **Intelligent-Tiering** moves each object between tiers automatically depending on use; good when you can't predict it.
- **Standard-IA** and **One Zone-IA** ("infrequent access") are cheaper to store, but charge per gigabyte read and for at least 30 days.
- **Glacier Instant Retrieval**, **Glacier Flexible Retrieval** and **Glacier Deep Archive** are for archives, with reads taking from milliseconds to hours.

**Lifecycle rules** move objects to cheaper classes, and later delete them, after a set number of days. A rule can apply to keys starting with a prefix like `logs/`, or to objects carrying a given label (tag).

**Versioning** keeps every old version of an object when it is overwritten or deleted, so mistakes can be undone (a delete just adds a "deleted" marker). Pair it with a lifecycle rule that removes old versions after a while, or costs grow quietly.

Large files are uploaded in parts, in parallel, by **multipart upload**; the CLI and SDKs do this automatically. Use `aws s3 sync` for whole directories and `aws s3api` for full control.
concepts.code:
B=acme-reports-111122223333
aws s3 mb "s3://$B" --region eu-west-1           # make a bucket
aws s3 cp report.csv "s3://$B/reports/2026/10/report.csv"
aws s3 sync ./site "s3://$B/site" --delete        # mirror a directory
aws s3 ls "s3://$B/reports/" --recursive --human-readable
# 2026-10-17 09:12:44   1.2 MiB reports/2026/10/report.csv

aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket "$B" \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# logs/: cheaper class after 30 days, archive after 180, delete after 2 years;
# old versions deleted 30 days after being replaced
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket "$B" \
  --lifecycle-configuration '{"Rules": [{
    "ID": "tier-logs", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": "logs/"},
    "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"},
                    {"Days": 180, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}],
    "Expiration": {"Days": 730},
    "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {"NoncurrentDays": 30}}]}'
takeaways: Buckets live in one Region with names unique across AWS; objects = key + bytes + metadata
Prefixes are just the start of key names, not folders
Choose storage classes by how often data is read; automate with lifecycle rules
Versioning protects data but needs a rule to delete old versions
pitfalls: Moving small, frequently read objects to Standard-IA, where per-read fees and minimums cost more than they save.

quiz.q: Right after an upload of a new object succeeds, your program reads it. What does S3 return?
options: Possibly "not found" for a few seconds
The new object, because S3 is strongly consistent
An error until copying to other AZs completes
quiz.explain: S3 guarantees that a read after a successful write sees the new data.

quiz.q: Data is written once, rarely read, and must be kept 7 years at the lowest cost. Which class fits?
quiz.explain: Deep Archive is the cheapest storage for long-term, rarely read data, with reads taking hours.

concepts.name: Block and file storage: EBS and EFS
concepts.summary: Attach EBS volumes to instances as disks, back them up with snapshots, and use EFS when many machines need the same shared folder.
concepts.why: Databases, build tools and older apps need real disks and file systems, and the wrong choice costs money or reliability.
concepts.body:
An EC2 instance needs a disk. **EBS** (Elastic Block Store) provides **volumes**: network-attached disks that look to the operating system like an ordinary hard drive (a **block device**, in Linux terms). A volume lives in **one AZ**, normally attaches to one instance at a time, and keeps its data on its own, even after the instance is gone.

Disks have two kinds of speed. **IOPS** is how many separate reads and writes they handle per second, which databases care about. **Throughput** is how many megabytes per second they move, which matters for big files.

Volume types:

- **gp3**: the default, an **SSD** (storage on chips, with no moving parts). It includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s whatever its size, and you can buy more of either separately. Prefer it to the older gp2, whose speed depended on its size.
- **io2 Block Express**: an SSD with very high guaranteed IOPS for demanding databases.
- **st1** and **sc1**: cheaper spinning hard disks, good at reading big files from start to end.

You can make a volume bigger or change its type while it's in use, then tell the operating system to grow its file system into the new space.

A **snapshot** is a saved copy of a volume at one moment. Each one stores only what changed since the previous one, which makes snapshots cheap **backups**. AWS keeps them in S3, its file storage, for the whole Region, so you can create a new volume from a snapshot in any AZ, or copy it to another Region in case a whole Region fails. A volume made from a snapshot fetches its data on first use, so first reads are slow.

Turn on **encryption** by default for EBS in each account; AWS Backup can take snapshots on a schedule.

**EFS** (Elastic File System) is a shared folder over the network that many instances and containers, in different AZs, can mount at the same time. It uses **NFS**, the standard way Linux machines share folders. It grows and shrinks by itself and you pay per gigabyte stored. Use it for shared files, not as a database's disk.

**Instance store** disks are inside the host machine: very fast, but wiped when the instance stops.
concepts.code:
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default

VOL=$(aws ec2 create-volume --availability-zone eu-west-1a --size 100 \
  --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 --throughput 250 --query VolumeId --output text)
aws ec2 wait volume-available --volume-ids "$VOL"
aws ec2 attach-volume --volume-id "$VOL" --instance-id i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 --device /dev/sdf

# Grow it while in use, then on the instance: sudo xfs_growfs /data
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id "$VOL" --size 200

SNAP=$(aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id "$VOL" --description nightly \
  --query SnapshotId --output text)
aws ec2 copy-snapshot --region eu-central-1 \
  --source-region eu-west-1 --source-snapshot-id "$SNAP"   # copy to another Region

# A shared folder for many instances or containers
aws efs create-file-system --encrypted --throughput-mode elastic \
  --tags Key=Name,Value=shared-media --query FileSystemId --output text
# fs-0a1b2c3d   ->  sudo mount -t efs fs-0a1b2c3d:/ /mnt/shared
takeaways: EBS = a disk in one AZ; gp3 is the default, with adjustable IOPS and throughput
Snapshots store only changes, cover the whole Region and can be copied to other Regions
EFS = one shared folder for many machines across AZs
Instance store is fast but temporary
pitfalls: Expecting an EBS volume to attach to an instance in another AZ; make a new volume there from a snapshot instead.

quiz.q: Ten containers in three AZs must read and write the same files. What should you use?
quiz.explain: EFS is a shared file system across AZs; an EBS volume lives in one AZ and normally attaches to one instance.

quiz.q: You need a volume's data in a different AZ. How?
options: Detach it and attach it to an instance there
Snapshot it and create a new volume from the snapshot in the target AZ
Change the volume's AZ with modify-volume
Copy it with aws s3 cp
quiz.explain: Volumes are tied to their AZ; snapshots cover the Region and can create volumes in any AZ.

concepts.name: RDS: managed relational databases
concepts.summary: Let AWS run PostgreSQL, MySQL and other databases for you, with automatic backups, a standby for failover, and read replicas for extra reads.
concepts.why: Most applications need a relational database, and RDS takes over the routine work of running one.
concepts.body:
Most applications keep their data in a **relational database**: tables of rows and columns, like linked spreadsheets, that programs search and change with **SQL**, a standard language (`SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = 42`). PostgreSQL and MySQL are popular examples.

**RDS** (Relational Database Service) runs such a database for you. You choose the **database engine**, meaning the database software (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server or Db2), the **instance class**, meaning the server size such as `db.m7g.large`, and the storage. AWS sets it up, installs updates in a weekly maintenance window, takes backups and watches its health. You never get access to the server itself.

Networking: put the database in a **DB subnet group**, a set of private subnets in at least two AZs. Keep it **not publicly accessible**, and allow its port only from the app servers' security group.

Connect using its **hostname**, which RDS calls the endpoint: a name such as `orders-db.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com`. **DNS**, the internet's phone book, turns that name into the database's current IP address. Never use the address itself, because it changes when the database moves to its standby.

Staying up and handling more reads are separate features:

- **Multi-AZ** keeps a **standby** copy in another AZ. Every write is copied to it before the write is confirmed (**synchronous** copying), so it never falls behind. If the main database or its AZ fails, RDS switches to the standby automatically, usually within a minute or two. That switch is called **failover**, and the hostname then points to the new main database. In the classic setup the standby can't serve reads.
- **Read replicas** are extra copies updated a moment after each write (**asynchronous** copying), possibly in other Regions. Your app can send reads, such as reports, to them to take load off the main database. They may lag slightly behind, and one can be promoted to a standalone database. Keeping copies like this is called **replication**.

**Backups**: RDS backs up automatically and records every change, so you can do a **point-in-time restore** to any second within the retention period you pick (up to 35 days). You can also take manual **snapshots**, saved copies kept until you delete them. A restore always creates a *new* database.

Also useful: `--manage-master-user-password` keeps the admin password in **Secrets Manager**, AWS's safe for passwords. Deletion protection stops accidental deletes. **RDS Proxy** shares a small pool of open connections among many short-lived clients such as Lambda functions, which could otherwise swamp the database.
concepts.code:
aws rds create-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name app-db \
  --db-subnet-group-description "Private DB subnets" \
  --subnet-ids subnet-db-a subnet-db-b

aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --engine postgres --db-instance-class db.m7g.large \
  --allocated-storage 100 --storage-type gp3 --storage-encrypted \
  --multi-az --no-publicly-accessible \
  --master-username app --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name app-db --vpc-security-group-ids sg-db \
  --backup-retention-period 7 --deletion-protection

aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier orders-db
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].Endpoint.Address' --output text
# orders-db.c1abc2def3gh.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com   <- connect to this name

aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica --db-instance-identifier orders-db-ro \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db
takeaways: RDS handles updates, backups and failover; you handle your tables, SQL and who can connect
Multi-AZ is for staying up; read replicas are for handling more reads
Private subnets, security-group-to-security-group access, connect by hostname
A point-in-time restore creates a new database
pitfalls: Expecting the classic Multi-AZ standby to serve reads; use read replicas for that.

quiz.q: The main database's AZ fails. What lets the application recover automatically?
options: A Multi-AZ deployment with automatic failover
A read replica in the same AZ
quiz.explain: Multi-AZ fails over to a standby that is always up to date and repoints the hostname.

quiz.q: Reports are slowing down the main database. What helps without changing how it fails over?
options: Add a read replica and send the reports to it
quiz.explain: Read replicas take reads off the main database; the classic Multi-AZ standby doesn't serve reads.

concepts.name: Lambda functions
concepts.summary: Run code without managing servers: write a handler, give it an execution role, and let events trigger it, paying only per request and run time.
concepts.why: Lambda is the glue, and often the core, of AWS systems: from the server side of websites to file processing and automation.
concepts.body:
**Serverless** means you hand AWS only your code, and AWS runs it when needed on machines you never see. You pay only while it runs. **Lambda** is AWS's main serverless service, and a Lambda function is your code plus a few settings.

You write a **handler**, a function AWS calls once for each event. In Python it looks like `def handler(event, context)`. `event` is a dict describing what happened: a web request, a new file being stored, or a group of messages waiting in a **queue** (a line of work items handled in order). `context` carries details such as how much time is left.

Settings that matter:

- **Runtime**: the language version AWS provides, such as `python3.13` or `nodejs22.x`. A function can also be a container image of up to 10 GB.
- Memory, from 128 MB to 10,240 MB. CPU power grows with memory, so more memory often runs faster for about the same cost.
- **Timeout**: the longest one run may take, at most 15 minutes. Longer jobs belong in other services.
- **Execution role**: the IAM role the function runs as, which decides what its code may do in AWS. Other settings go in environment variables.
- The processor type, its **CPU architecture**: `arm64`, AWS's own **Graviton** chips, is usually cheaper than `x86_64`, the type in most PCs.

How a function is called depends on what triggers it:

- **Synchronous**: the caller waits for the answer. A web request arriving through **API Gateway** (an AWS service that gives functions web addresses) or a **function URL** (a web address, or **URL**, for one function) works this way.
- **Asynchronous**: AWS stores the event and answers the sender at once, then runs the function. If it fails, Lambda **retries** twice. Notifications about newly stored files work this way.
- Reading a queue: Lambda fetches messages itself and calls the function with groups of them. This is an **event source mapping**.

Each copy of a function runs in its own small sandbox, an **execution environment**. If ten requests arrive at once, ten environments run side by side; that number is the function's **concurrency**.

Starting a new environment, and running your file's top-level code, takes extra time: a **cold start**. Later requests reuse the warm environment. So do slow setup, such as creating an SDK client, outside the handler, but never keep one request's data in global variables, because the next request will see it.

Whatever you `print` or log goes to **CloudWatch** Logs, AWS's log store, automatically. To deploy, zip the code and run `aws lambda create-function` with the runtime, handler, zip file and execution role (see the code).
concepts.code:
# app.py
import json

INVOCATIONS = 0   # top level: kept between calls in a warm environment

def handler(event, context):
    global INVOCATIONS
    INVOCATIONS += 1
    name = (event.get("queryStringParameters") or {}).get("name", "world")
    return {                       # a web response; 200 means OK
        "statusCode": 200,
        "headers": {"content-type": "application/json"},
        "body": json.dumps({"hello": name, "invocation": INVOCATIONS}),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":   # quick local test
    print(handler({"queryStringParameters": {"name": "Ada"}}, None)["body"])
    # {"hello": "Ada", "invocation": 1}

# Deploy and call it:
# zip fn.zip app.py
# aws lambda create-function --function-name hello --runtime python3.13 \
#   --architectures arm64 --handler app.handler --zip-file fileb://fn.zip \
#   --role arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/orders-fn
# aws lambda invoke --function-name hello --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \
#   --payload '{"queryStringParameters": {"name": "Ada"}}' out.json
takeaways: handler(event, context); the event's shape depends on what triggered it
Memory also sets CPU; the timeout is at most 15 minutes
Setup code outside the handler runs once per execution environment
Synchronous, asynchronous and queue-reading calls behave differently
pitfalls: Keeping one request's data in global variables, which leaks into later requests in a warm environment.

quiz.q: Where should you create an AWS SDK client that every call of the function uses?
options: At the top level of the file, outside the handler
In a separate file read on every call
quiz.explain: Top-level code runs once per execution environment and is reused by later warm calls.

quiz.q: A CPU-heavy function with 128 MB of memory takes 8 seconds. What is a sensible first experiment?
options: Allow more copies to run at once
Increase memory, which also increases CPU
quiz.explain: CPU is given in proportion to memory, so more memory can cut run time and even cost.

concepts.name: How AWS pricing works
concepts.summary: Learn what AWS charges for (compute time, storage, requests, data transfer), set budget alerts, and find out what is costing money.
concepts.why: Cloud bills follow from design choices; engineers who understand pricing avoid nasty surprises.
concepts.body:
AWS charges for what you use, along a few recurring kinds of charge:

- **Compute time**: per second or hour for virtual machines, containers and databases. Lambda charges per request plus per gigabyte-second (memory multiplied by run time).
- **Storage**: per gigabyte per month for files, disks and **backups** (saved copies), sometimes plus a fee for guaranteed disk speed.
- **Requests**: many services charge per API call, such as each upload to or read from file storage.
- **Data transfer**: data coming into AWS from the internet is free; data going out to the internet is charged per gigabyte; traffic between AZs is charged in both directions; traffic between Regions is charged too.

Some charges surprise people because nothing seems to be running:

- **NAT gateways**, the devices that let private servers reach the internet: charged per hour and per gigabyte.
- Public **IPv4 addresses**, the numbers machines are reached at from the internet: charged per hour.
- Disks attached to nothing, and old **snapshots** (saved disk copies).
- Logs kept forever, idle **load balancers** (machines that spread traffic across servers), and forgotten test databases.

Tools to keep spending in check:

- The AWS Pricing Calculator, to estimate before you build.
- **AWS Budgets**, which emails you when actual or forecast spending passes a limit. Create one on day one.
- **Cost Explorer**, which breaks spending down by service, account, Region or tag.
- **Free Tier**: new accounts get free credits, and some services include a free monthly amount, such as a million Lambda requests.

Tags are labels you attach to resources, like `team=search`. To see costs split by a tag, you must first turn it on as a **cost allocation tag** in the billing console, and it only counts from then on.

Prices differ by Region and change over time, so check each service's pricing page rather than memorising numbers.
concepts.code:
# Email when forecast monthly spend exceeds 80% of $200
aws budgets create-budget --account-id 111122223333 \
  --budget '{"BudgetName": "monthly-total", "BudgetType": "COST", "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
             "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "200", "Unit": "USD"}}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{
     "Notification": {"NotificationType": "FORECASTED", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
                      "Threshold": 80, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
     "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "ops@example.com"}]}]'

# Cost Explorer: the five most expensive services last month
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[].[Keys[0],Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount]' \
  --output text | sort -t$'\t' -k2 -nr | head -5

# Classic waste: disks attached to nothing
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query 'Volumes[].[VolumeId,Size,VolumeType]' --output text
takeaways: Bills = compute time + storage + requests + data transfer
Traffic out to the internet, between AZs and between Regions costs money
Set a budget alert immediately; use Cost Explorer and activated tags to see who spends what
Watch idle things: NAT gateways, public IPv4 addresses, loose disks, old logs
pitfalls: Keeping logs forever ('never expire'), paying to store data nobody reads.

quiz.q: Which traffic is normally free?
options: Data from a virtual machine out to the internet
Data coming into AWS from the internet
quiz.explain: Incoming data is free; outgoing, cross-AZ and cross-Region transfer are charged.

quiz.q: You tag resources with team=search but the tag doesn't appear in Cost Explorer. Why?
options: Cost allocation tags must be activated in the billing console first
Tags only work on virtual machines
Tags take a year to appear
Cost Explorer can't group by tag
quiz.explain: Your own tags must be activated as cost allocation tags, and count only from then on.

concepts.name: CloudWatch metrics, logs and alarms
concepts.summary: Collect metrics and logs in CloudWatch, search logs with Logs Insights, and set alarms on what matters.
concepts.why: You can't run what you can't see; CloudWatch is where AWS services report their health by default.
concepts.body:
**CloudWatch** is AWS's **monitoring** service: it collects measurements and logs from your resources and warns you when something looks wrong.

A **metric** is one measurement tracked over time, such as an instance's CPU use each minute; a list of values over time like that is a **time series**. A metric is identified by a **namespace** (a category such as `AWS/EC2`, or one of your own), a name (`CPUUtilization`) and dimensions: labels saying which resource it is about, such as `InstanceId`.

AWS services publish metrics automatically: EC2 every 5 minutes (every minute if you pay for detailed monitoring), most others every minute. EC2 can't see memory or disk use inside the operating system, so install the CloudWatch agent on the instance for those. You can also publish your own numbers, such as orders placed, with `put-metric-data`.

A **CloudWatch alarm** watches one metric and is in one of three states: `OK`, `ALARM`, or `INSUFFICIENT_DATA` (not enough data yet). Make it need "M out of N" bad readings, say 3 of the last 5 minutes, so one brief spike doesn't set it off.
