VPC CNI gives pods VPC IPs: plan subnet sizes
Access entries map IAM to cluster access; Pod Identity maps pods to IAM roles
Budget for upgrades every few months
pitfalls: Granting application permissions to the node instance role, which every pod on the node can use.

quiz.q: How should a pod get permission to read an S3 bucket on EKS?
options: Associate its service account with an IAM role via Pod Identity or IRSA
Add the permission to the node group's instance role
Mount access keys as a Kubernetes secret
Use the cluster's control plane role
quiz.explain: Pod-level IAM scopes permissions to one service account instead of the whole node.

quiz.q: Pods fail to schedule with errors about no free IP addresses. What is the likely cause?
options: VPC CNI assigns VPC IPs to pods and the subnets are too small
quiz.explain: Each pod consumes a VPC IP, so small subnets run out quickly.

concepts.name: Aurora architecture and Serverless v2
concepts.summary: Understand Aurora's shared distributed storage, cluster endpoints, fast failover, Serverless v2 scaling and cloning.
concepts.why: Aurora is the default high-end relational option on AWS, and its architecture changes how you think about replicas and failover.
concepts.body:
**Aurora** is AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine with a redesigned storage layer. Instead of each instance owning a disk, a cluster has one **shared, distributed storage volume** that keeps six copies of the data across three AZs and grows automatically. Writes need four of six copies and reads three, so losing an entire AZ (plus one more copy) doesn't lose data.

Compute is separate: one **writer** and up to 15 **readers** in any AZs, all reading the same storage. Replicas don't replay a full copy of the data, so replica lag is usually milliseconds, and any reader can be promoted.

**Endpoints**: the *cluster endpoint* always points to the writer, the *reader endpoint* load-balances across readers, and custom endpoints group specific instances (for example, analytics readers). Failover promotes a reader, usually within a minute or less; give readers failover priorities and run at least one reader in another AZ.

**Serverless v2** instances (`db.serverless`) scale capacity in fine-grained Aurora Capacity Units between a minimum and maximum, and can mix with provisioned instances in the same cluster. Scale-to-zero is supported for idle dev databases.

Other features worth knowing:

- **Fast cloning**: copy-on-write clones of a whole cluster in minutes, ideal for testing on production-like data.
- **Global Database**: storage-level replication to other Regions, typically under a second of lag.
- **I/O-Optimized** storage removes per-I/O charges, cheaper when I/O is a large part of the bill.
- Backtrack (MySQL) rewinds a cluster in place without restoring.
concepts.code:
aws rds create-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier orders \
  --engine aurora-postgresql --storage-type aurora-iopt1 --storage-encrypted \
  --serverless-v2-scaling-configuration MinCapacity=0.5,MaxCapacity=16 \
  --master-username app --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name app-db --vpc-security-group-ids sg-db

for i in 1 2; do   # writer + reader; RDS spreads them across AZs
  aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "orders-$i" \
    --db-cluster-identifier orders --engine aurora-postgresql \
    --db-instance-class db.serverless
done

aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].[Endpoint,ReaderEndpoint]' --output text
# orders.cluster-c1abc.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com  orders.cluster-ro-c1abc.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com

aws rds failover-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier orders   # rehearse failover

# Copy-on-write clone for testing
aws rds restore-db-cluster-to-point-in-time --db-cluster-identifier orders-test \
  --source-db-cluster-identifier orders --restore-type copy-on-write \
  --use-latest-restorable-time
takeaways: One shared six-way storage volume across three AZs; compute is separate
Writer plus up to 15 readers with millisecond lag; cluster and reader endpoints
Serverless v2 scales capacity in ACUs, including to zero for idle clusters
Clones, Global Database and I/O-Optimized storage are key differentiators
pitfalls: Running a single Aurora instance and assuming the storage replication makes compute highly available too.

quiz.q: Why is Aurora replica lag usually much lower than RDS read-replica lag?
options: Aurora uses synchronous replication to readers
Readers share the same storage volume instead of replaying changes into their own copy
Readers are in the same AZ
quiz.explain: Aurora readers read the shared storage, so they only need to update cached pages.

quiz.q: Your app writes through the reader endpoint by mistake. What happens?
options: Writes are forwarded to the writer automatically
Writes succeed on the reader and replicate
Writes fail, because readers are read-only
quiz.explain: Reader instances are read-only; writes must go through the cluster (writer) endpoint.

concepts.name: DynamoDB data modeling at scale
concepts.summary: Design from access patterns: single-table layouts, GSIs, hot-partition avoidance, conditional writes, transactions and Streams.
concepts.why: DynamoDB rewards up-front modeling and punishes relational habits; good key design is the difference between fast and throttled.
concepts.body:
DynamoDB modeling starts from **access patterns**, not entities. List every query the app makes, then design keys so each is a `GetItem` or a single `Query`.

**Single-table design** stores several entity types together with generic keys: `PK=CUSTOMER#42, SK=PROFILE` and `PK=CUSTOMER#42, SK=ORDER#2026-10-02#A17`. One Query on `CUSTOMER#42` returns the customer and their orders, the DynamoDB equivalent of a join. Many teams prefer one table per bounded context; the principle that matters is pre-joining data that is read together.

**Secondary indexes** add access patterns:

- **GSIs** have their own partition and sort keys, are eventually consistent, can be added any time, and project only the attributes you choose. *Sparse* GSIs index only items that have the key attribute, giving cheap filtered lists.
- **LSIs** share the table's partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, and cap each item collection at 10 GB. Prefer GSIs.

**Throughput**: each physical partition serves up to about 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second. Adaptive capacity helps, but a single hot key (a global counter, today's date as partition key) still throttles. Spread writes with high-cardinality keys or write sharding (`DATE#2026-10-17#7`).

**Correctness tools**: conditional writes for uniqueness (`attribute_not_exists(PK)`) and **optimistic locking** with a version attribute; `TransactWriteItems` for all-or-nothing changes across up to 100 items (at double cost); **Streams** to react to changes with Lambda, for projections, search indexing or events. For ad-hoc analytics, export to S3 rather than scanning.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

t = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name="eu-west-1").create_table(
    TableName="app", BillingMode="PAY_PER_REQUEST",
    KeySchema=[{"AttributeName": "PK", "KeyType": "HASH"}, {"AttributeName": "SK", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
    AttributeDefinitions=[{"AttributeName": a, "AttributeType": "S"} for a in ("PK", "SK")])
t.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUSTOMER#42", "SK": "PROFILE", "name": "Ada", "ver": 1})
t.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUSTOMER#42", "SK": "ORDER#2026-10-02#A17", "total": 35})

def rename(new_name, expected_ver):   # optimistic locking
    try:
        t.update_item(Key={"PK": "CUSTOMER#42", "SK": "PROFILE"},
            UpdateExpression="SET #n = :n, ver = ver + :one",
            ConditionExpression="ver = :v", ExpressionAttributeNames={"#n": "name"},
            ExpressionAttributeValues={":n": new_name, ":v": expected_ver, ":one": 1})
        return "ok"
    except ClientError as e:
        return e.response["Error"]["Code"]

print(rename("Ada L.", 1))   # ok
print(rename("Ada K.", 1))   # ConditionalCheckFailedException (stale version)
items = t.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("PK").eq("CUSTOMER#42"))["Items"]
print([i["SK"] for i in items])   # ['ORDER#2026-10-02#A17', 'PROFILE']
takeaways: List access patterns first, then design keys and indexes for them
Store data read together under one partition key
GSIs add access patterns; hot keys throttle regardless of table capacity
Use conditional writes, transactions and Streams for correctness and reactions
pitfalls: Using a low-cardinality partition key such as status or today's date, concentrating traffic on one partition.

quiz.q: Two users load version 3 of a profile and both save. How do you stop the second save silently overwriting the first?
options: Make the update conditional on ver = 3 and increment it
quiz.explain: Optimistic locking makes the second write fail with ConditionalCheckFailedException.

quiz.q: You must query orders by status across all customers. What is the usual approach?
options: Add a GSI keyed on status (sharded if needed) with the order date as sort key
Scan the table with a filter
Store all orders under one partition key
quiz.explain: A GSI provides the new access pattern; LSIs can't change the partition key and must exist at creation.

concepts.name: Lambda at scale: concurrency and batching
concepts.summary: Control concurrency, tame cold starts, process SQS batches with partial failures, and make functions idempotent.
concepts.why: Production serverless systems fail at the edges: throttles, retries, duplicate events and cold starts.
concepts.body:
**Concurrency** is the number of execution environments serving requests at once. Accounts have a regional limit (1,000 by default, raisable) shared by all functions.

- **Reserved concurrency** guarantees a function capacity and also caps it, which protects downstream systems such as a database. Setting it to 0 pauses the function.
- **Provisioned concurrency** keeps environments initialised ahead of time to remove cold starts, billed while configured.
- Beyond the limit, synchronous calls are throttled (429) and async events are retried.

**Cold starts** are the init phase of a new environment. Reduce them with small deployment packages, lazy imports, `arm64`, avoiding heavy frameworks at import time, and **SnapStart** (Java, Python, .NET), which restores from a snapshot of an initialised environment.

**SQS event source mappings** poll for you. Tune `BatchSize`, `MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds` and `ScalingConfig.MaximumConcurrency` (to limit how many functions the queue drives). By default, one failure fails the whole batch and every message is retried; enable **ReportBatchItemFailures** and return the failed message IDs so only those return to the queue. Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout.

**Async invocations** retry up to two times; configure maximum event age and **on-failure destinations** (SQS, SNS, EventBridge, S3) to capture what still fails.

Because every source can deliver duplicates, make handlers **idempotent**: dedupe on a business key with a conditional DynamoDB write, or use the idempotency utility in Powertools for AWS Lambda, which also provides structured logging, metrics and tracing.
takeaways: Reserved concurrency guarantees and caps; provisioned concurrency pre-warms
Use ReportBatchItemFailures so one bad message doesn't retry the whole batch
Visibility timeout at least 6x the function timeout
Every event source can duplicate: build idempotent handlers
pitfalls: Letting a queue scale Lambda to hundreds of concurrent functions that exhaust a relational database's connections.

quiz.q: A batch of 10 SQS messages has one bad message and partial batch responses are not enabled. What happens?
options: Only the bad message is retried
The whole batch becomes visible again and all 10 are retried
quiz.explain: Without ReportBatchItemFailures, any error fails the batch and every message returns to the queue.

quiz.q: You must ensure a function never runs more than 20 copies at once, to protect a database. What do you set?
options: Reserved concurrency of 20 (or MaximumConcurrency on the SQS mapping)
quiz.explain: Reserved concurrency (or the SQS mapping's maximum concurrency) caps parallel executions.

concepts.name: AWS CDK: infrastructure in code
concepts.summary: Define stacks with constructs in Python or TypeScript, use L2 constructs and grant methods, and deploy via synthesized CloudFormation.
concepts.why: CDK gives you loops, types, tests and reusable components for infrastructure while keeping CloudFormation's safety.
concepts.body:
The **AWS CDK** (v2, package `aws-cdk-lib`) lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, C# or Go. Your program builds a tree: an **App** contains **Stacks**, which contain **constructs**. `cdk synth` turns it into CloudFormation templates, and `cdk deploy` deploys them as stacks.

Construct levels:

- **L1** (`CfnBucket`, `CfnQueue`): a one-to-one mapping of CloudFormation resources.
- **L2** (`s3.Bucket`, `lambda_.Function`): curated APIs with secure defaults and helper methods.
- **L3 patterns** (such as `ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService`): whole architectures in one construct.

The killer feature is **grants**: `table.grant_read_write_data(fn)` adds a least-privilege IAM policy to the function's role, scoped to that table. Similar methods connect security groups, event sources and KMS keys.

Workflow: run `cdk bootstrap` once per account and Region (it creates the asset bucket, ECR repository and deployment roles), then `cdk diff` to preview and `cdk deploy`. Assets such as Lambda code and Docker images are packaged and uploaded automatically.

Things that bite:

- A construct's **ID path** determines the CloudFormation logical ID. Renaming or moving a construct means delete-and-recreate, which for a table means data loss unless retained.
- Stateful L2 resources often default to `RemovalPolicy.RETAIN`; be explicit.
- Keep stacks deterministic: no API lookups at synth time without caching them in `cdk.context.json`.

Test with `aws_cdk.assertions.Template.from_stack(...)` and add **Aspects** or cdk-nag for policy checks.
concepts.code:
from aws_cdk import App, Duration, Environment, RemovalPolicy, Stack
from aws_cdk import aws_dynamodb as ddb, aws_lambda as lambda_, aws_sqs as sqs
from aws_cdk.aws_lambda_event_sources import SqsEventSource
from constructs import Construct

class OrdersStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, id: str, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(scope, id, **kwargs)
        table = ddb.TableV2(self, "Orders", removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,
            partition_key=ddb.Attribute(name="PK", type=ddb.AttributeType.STRING),
            sort_key=ddb.Attribute(name="SK", type=ddb.AttributeType.STRING))
        queue = sqs.Queue(self, "Incoming", visibility_timeout=Duration.seconds(180))
        fn = lambda_.Function(self, "Worker", runtime=lambda_.Runtime.PYTHON_3_13,
            architecture=lambda_.Architecture.ARM_64, handler="app.handler",
            code=lambda_.Code.from_asset("src"), timeout=Duration.seconds(30),
            environment={"TABLE": table.table_name})
        fn.add_event_source(SqsEventSource(queue, batch_size=10, report_batch_item_failures=True))
        table.grant_read_write_data(fn)   # least-privilege IAM, generated

app = App()
OrdersStack(app, "orders-dev", env=Environment(account="111122223333", region="eu-west-1"))
app.synth()
# cdk bootstrap aws://111122223333/eu-west-1 && cdk diff && cdk deploy orders-dev
takeaways: CDK code synthesizes to CloudFormation; stacks deploy as usual
Prefer L2 constructs; use grant methods for least-privilege IAM
Bootstrap each account/Region once; cdk diff before deploy
Construct IDs become logical IDs: renaming replaces resources
pitfalls: Refactoring construct names or nesting, which silently changes logical IDs and replaces stateful resources.

quiz.q: What does table.grant_read_write_data(fn) do?
options: Adds an IAM policy to fn's role allowing data reads and writes on that table only
Copies the table into the function
quiz.explain: Grant methods generate scoped IAM statements on the grantee's role.

quiz.q: You move a DynamoDB table construct into a new parent construct. What can happen on deploy?
options: Its logical ID changes, so CloudFormation creates a new table and removes (or orphans) the old one
quiz.explain: Logical IDs derive from the construct path; changing it looks like a different resource.

concepts.name: Cost optimization in practice
concepts.summary: Cut spend with rightsizing, Savings Plans, Spot, Graviton, storage tiering and data-transfer-aware architecture, and catch anomalies early.
concepts.why: At scale, a few architectural and purchasing decisions routinely save 30 to 60 percent of a cloud bill.
concepts.body:
Cost optimization works in a loop: **see** spend, **reduce** waste, **commit** for discounts, and **architect** for efficiency.

**Visibility**: tag consistently and activate the tags, export detailed billing data (CUR 2.0 via Data Exports) to query with Athena, and enable **Cost Anomaly Detection** to get alerted when a service's spend jumps. Track unit costs, such as cost per order, not just the total.

**Waste**: idle and oversized resources. **Compute Optimizer** recommends instance, EBS, Lambda and ECS sizes from measured use. Schedule non-production environments off at night, delete unattached volumes, old snapshots and AMIs, and migrate gp2 volumes to gp3.

**Purchase options**:

- **Savings Plans**: commit to a dollar amount per hour for 1 or 3 years. *Compute Savings Plans* (up to about 66% off) apply flexibly across EC2 families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda; *EC2 Instance Savings Plans* (up to about 72%) are tied to a family in a Region. Cover the steady baseline, not peaks.
- **Reserved Instances** remain the mechanism for RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Redshift.
- **Spot** capacity is up to 90% cheaper but can be reclaimed with a 2-minute warning. Use it for stateless, fault-tolerant work: CI runners, batch jobs, containers. Diversify instance types and use capacity-optimised allocation.

**Architecture**: Graviton instances and `arm64` Lambdas; S3 Intelligent-Tiering and lifecycle rules; gateway endpoints instead of NAT for S3 traffic; CloudFront in front of your servers so repeat requests never reach them; same-AZ traffic where it is safe; sensible log retention; and serverless for spiky, low-volume workloads.
concepts.code:
# Rightsizing findings from Compute Optimizer
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \
  --query 'instanceRecommendations[].[instanceArn,finding,recommendationOptions[0].instanceType]' \
  --output text
# arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:111122223333:instance/i-0a1b...  Overprovisioned  m7g.large

# What Compute Savings Plan commitment would AWS suggest?
aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP \
  --term-in-years ONE_YEAR --payment-option NO_UPFRONT --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS \
  --query 'SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendation.SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendationSummary.[HourlyCommitmentToPurchase,EstimatedSavingsPercentage]'

# gp2 -> gp3: same or better performance, lower price, online
for v in $(aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=volume-type,Values=gp2 \
             --query 'Volumes[].VolumeId' --output text); do
  aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id "$v" --volume-type gp3
done

# Alert on unusual spend per service
aws ce create-anomaly-monitor --anomaly-monitor \
  '{"MonitorName": "per-service", "MonitorType": "DIMENSIONAL", "MonitorDimension": "SERVICE"}'
takeaways: Loop: visibility, waste removal, commitments, architecture
Savings Plans cover the steady baseline; Spot for interruptible work
Rightsize with Compute Optimizer; move to Graviton and gp3
Data transfer and NAT are architecture problems, not purchasing ones
pitfalls: Buying commitments for peak usage, leaving them under-used when load drops.

quiz.q: A fleet runs steadily on EC2, Fargate and Lambda and might move Regions next year. Which commitment fits?
quiz.explain: Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda.

quiz.q: Which workload is the best fit for Spot?
options: The only NAT instance in a VPC
A licensed server tied to one host
quiz.explain: Spot can be reclaimed at short notice, so it suits interruptible, stateless work.

concepts.name: Well-Architected and resilience design
concepts.summary: Apply the six Well-Architected pillars and pick a disaster-recovery strategy from RPO and RTO targets.
concepts.why: A shared framework for trade-offs keeps designs reviewable, and DR strategy determines what an outage costs you.
concepts.body:
The **AWS Well-Architected Framework** organises design questions into six pillars:

- **Operational excellence**: infrastructure as code, small reversible changes, good visibility into running systems, runbooks.
- **Security**: strong identity, least privilege, traceability, encryption, protection at every layer.
- **Reliability**: recover automatically, add capacity by adding machines, test recovery, manage change.
- **Performance efficiency**: the right resource types, serverless where it fits, measure and experiment.
- **Cost optimization**: pay only for what you need and know who spends what.
- **Sustainability**: keep resources busy and use as few as possible.

The free **Well-Architected Tool** walks a workload through these questions (plus lenses such as Serverless and SaaS) and tracks improvement items.

For resilience, start within a Region: spread across at least two AZs, keep compute stateless behind load balancers, use managed Multi-AZ data stores, and design for **static stability**, meaning the system keeps working through an AZ loss with capacity already in place rather than needing to launch new resources mid-incident.

For disaster recovery, define two targets per workload: **RPO** (recovery point objective: how much data you can lose) and **RTO** (recovery time objective: how long you can be down). Then pick a strategy, in rising cost:

- **Backup and restore**: hours of RTO; backups copied to another Region.
- **Pilot light**: data replicated continuously, core infrastructure defined but scaled to zero.
- **Warm standby**: a scaled-down, fully working copy ready to scale up.
- **Multi-site active/active**: near-zero RTO, the most complex and expensive.

A DR plan you haven't tested is a hope, not a plan: rehearse restores and failovers regularly.
takeaways: Six pillars: operations, security, reliability, performance, cost, sustainability
Multi-AZ and static stability first; multi-Region for disaster recovery
RPO = acceptable data loss, RTO = acceptable downtime; they pick the DR strategy
Test recovery regularly
pitfalls: Treating backups that have never been restored as a disaster-recovery plan.

quiz.q: A system can lose up to 24 hours of data and be down for a day. Which DR strategy is most cost-effective?
quiz.explain: Generous RPO and RTO targets are met by the cheapest strategy, backup and restore.

quiz.q: What does static stability mean for an AZ failure?
options: Enough capacity is already running in the remaining AZs, so recovery doesn't depend on launching new resources
Traffic is stopped until the AZ recovers
All data is stored in one AZ
quiz.explain: Statically stable systems keep working without control-plane actions during the failure.

concepts.name: Multi-account with Organizations
concepts.summary: Structure many accounts into OUs, apply guardrails with SCPs, centralise identity and logging, and vend accounts with Control Tower.
concepts.why: Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary in AWS, and every serious AWS estate is a multi-account organization.
concepts.body:
**AWS Organizations** groups accounts under a **management account** (which pays the bill and should run no workloads). Accounts are arranged in **organizational units** (OUs), such as Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/Dev and Sandbox, and policies attached to an OU apply to everything below it.

Why many accounts: a problem in one can't spread to the others, prod and non-prod stay separate, quotas are independent, costs are visible per team, and permissions stay simpler. Consolidated billing still gives one invoice with shared volume discounts and Savings Plans.

**Service control policies** (SCPs) set the maximum permissions for every principal in member accounts, including their root users. They never grant anything. Typical guardrails: deny leaving the organization, deny turning off CloudTrail, GuardDuty or AWS Config, restrict Regions, and deny creating IAM users with access keys.

**Resource control policies** (RCPs) instead cap what can be done *to* resources such as S3 buckets and KMS keys, for example refusing access from outside the organization. Other policy types cover tags, backups and service settings.

Around it you build a **landing zone**, usually with **AWS Control Tower**: a log-archive account receiving organization CloudTrail and Config data, an audit/security account as **delegated administrator** for GuardDuty and Security Hub, preventive and detective controls, and **Account Factory** for creating new accounts with baselines.

People sign in through **IAM Identity Center**, where permission sets (such as ReadOnly or Developer) are assigned to groups per account. Deploy shared resources to many accounts with service-managed CloudFormation **StackSets**, and share networks with AWS RAM.
takeaways: Management account pays and governs; workloads live in member accounts grouped by OU
SCPs cap principals, RCPs cap resources; neither grants permissions
Landing zone: log archive, security tooling, Identity Center, account vending
Exempt global services when restricting Regions
pitfalls: A Region-deny SCP without exemptions for global services like IAM and STS, which breaks sign-in and IAM in every account.

quiz.q: An SCP on the Prod OU allows only s3:* and ec2:*. A role in a prod account has AdministratorAccess. What can it do?
quiz.explain: Effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP ceiling and the identity's policies.

quiz.q: Which account's principals are NOT restricted by SCPs?
quiz.explain: SCPs never apply to the management account, which is one reason to keep workloads out of it.

concepts.name: Policy evaluation logic in depth
concepts.summary: How AWS combines SCPs, RCPs, resource policies, identity policies, permission boundaries and session policies into one decision.
concepts.why: Debugging AccessDenied in multi-account setups, and designing guardrails, requires knowing exactly which layer said no.
concepts.body:
For each request AWS gathers every applicable policy and decides:

- Any **explicit Deny** in any of them ends it: denied.
- **SCPs** (on the principal's account) and **RCPs** (on the resource's account) from AWS Organizations must allow the action. They never grant anything; they cap what is possible, and don't apply to the management account.
- The **resource-based policy** and the **identity-based policy** grant access. Within one account, an Allow in either is usually enough. **Across accounts, both must allow**: the caller's identity policy and the resource's policy.
- A **permissions boundary** on the user or role caps its identity-based permissions; an action outside it is implicitly denied.
- **Session policies** passed when assuming a role or federating cap that session further.

Some resources are stricter. A **KMS key policy** must allow access (directly or by delegating to the account), otherwise IAM policies have no effect. A role's **trust policy** must allow the assume call.

Useful condition keys for guardrails: `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (only principals in my organization), `aws:ResourceOrgID`, and `aws:SourceArn` / `aws:SourceAccount` on policies that grant to service principals, which prevents a service from being tricked into acting on your resource for someone else (the confused deputy).

Beware `NotAction` with Allow (it grants everything else, including future actions) and `NotPrincipal`. The error message often names the policy type that denied the request. Test with the IAM policy simulator, which covers identity policies, boundaries and SCPs but not every resource policy, so confirm with a real call.
concepts.code:
# Which actions would this role be allowed to perform?
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/app \
  --action-names s3:GetObject s3:DeleteObject \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::acme-data/reports/q1.csv \
  --query 'EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]' --output text
# s3:GetObject     allowed
# s3:DeleteObject  explicitDeny

# A bucket policy guardrail: only principals from our organization
cat > org-only.json <<'EOF'
{"Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [{"Sid": "OrgOnly", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*",
   "Action": "s3:*",
   "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-data", "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data/*"],
   "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-a1b2c3d4e5"},
                 "Bool": {"aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"}}}]}
EOF
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket acme-data --policy file://org-only.json
takeaways: Explicit deny anywhere wins; SCPs, RCPs, boundaries and session policies only cap
Cross-account access needs both the identity policy and the resource policy
KMS key policies and role trust policies must allow on their own
Use aws:PrincipalOrgID and aws:SourceArn for data-perimeter guardrails
pitfalls: Expecting an SCP Allow to grant permissions; it only defines the maximum.

quiz.q: A role in account A has s3:GetObject on a bucket in account B, but the bucket policy says nothing about A. What happens?
options: Denied, because cross-account access needs the bucket policy to allow it too
Allowed, because the identity policy allows it
Denied, because roles cannot access other accounts
quiz.explain: Cross-account requests need an Allow on both the identity side and the resource side.

quiz.q: A permissions boundary allows only s3:* and the role's identity policy allows s3:* and ec2:*. What can the role do?
quiz.explain: Effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary.

concepts.name: KMS in depth: key policies, grants, context
concepts.summary: Key policies, grants, encryption context, Bucket Keys, multi-Region keys and request quotas: what breaks KMS at scale.
concepts.why: KMS sits on the hot path of every encrypted read and write, so policy mistakes or throttling become outages.
concepts.body:
Every KMS key has exactly one **key policy**, and it is authoritative. The default policy contains a statement allowing the account principal (`arn:aws:iam::<account>:root`) `kms:*`, which *delegates* to IAM: only then do IAM policies in that account matter. Remove it and only principals named in the key policy can use the key, which can lock you out.

**Cross-account** use requires the key policy to allow the other account and that account's IAM policies to allow its principals. Only customer managed keys can be shared this way.

**Grants** are fine-grained, revocable delegations created via the API, used heavily by services (an EBS volume attached to an instance works through a grant).

**Encryption context** is a set of non-secret key-value pairs bound to the ciphertext as authenticated data: decryption fails unless the same context is supplied. It appears in CloudTrail and can be required in policies with `kms:EncryptionContext:` conditions. `kms:ViaService` restricts use to calls made through a particular service.

**Quotas**: cryptographic requests share a per-account, per-Region rate (thousands to tens of thousands per second depending on Region). High-volume S3 SSE-KMS workloads can throttle; **S3 Bucket Keys** derive a bucket-level key and cut KMS calls dramatically, and the Encryption SDK can cache data keys.

**Multi-Region keys** share key material across Regions so ciphertext can be decrypted elsewhere without a call back. Deleting a key has a 7 to 30 day waiting period; disable it first and watch CloudTrail for usage, because data encrypted under a deleted key is unrecoverable.
takeaways: The key policy is authoritative; IAM only counts if it delegates to the account
Grants give revocable, programmatic access; services rely on them
Encryption context must match on decrypt and is logged in CloudTrail
Use S3 Bucket Keys or data-key caching to stay under KMS request quotas
pitfalls: Editing a key policy and dropping the account-root statement, locking out every IAM admin.

quiz.q: An IAM policy grants kms:Decrypt on a key, but the key policy has no account-root statement and doesn't name the role. Can the role decrypt?
options: Yes, IAM policies are always sufficient
No, the key policy must allow it directly or delegate to IAM
Yes, if the role is in the same account
quiz.explain: For KMS, IAM policies take effect only if the key policy delegates to the account.

quiz.q: A data lake with SSE-KMS gets ThrottlingException from KMS during heavy reads. What helps most?
options: Switch to an AWS managed key
quiz.explain: Bucket Keys reduce per-object KMS requests by using a bucket-level derived key.

concepts.name: Transit Gateway and hybrid networking
concepts.summary: Connect many VPCs, accounts and on-premises networks through a regional hub with segmented routing.
concepts.why: Beyond a handful of VPCs, peering meshes become unmanageable; Transit Gateway is the standard hub for enterprise AWS networks.
concepts.body:
**VPC peering** connects two VPCs privately but is non-transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C. With dozens of VPCs a full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 peerings.

A **Transit Gateway** (TGW) is a regional, highly available router. You create **attachments**: VPCs (via one subnet per AZ), Site-to-Site VPNs, Direct Connect gateways, peering to TGWs in other Regions, and Connect attachments for SD-WAN appliances. Share one TGW to all accounts through **AWS RAM**.

Routing has two separate ideas, and confusing them is the classic mistake:

- **Association**: each attachment is associated with exactly one TGW route table, which is used to look up where *its* traffic goes.
- **Propagation**: an attachment can propagate its CIDRs into any number of route tables, so others learn how to reach it.

Multiple route tables give **segmentation**: prod and dev VPCs associate with different tables, both learn routes to a shared-services VPC, but not to each other. Static routes and blackhole routes add control. The VPCs' own subnet route tables still need routes pointing to the TGW.

Common patterns: **centralised egress** (one NAT VPC for the organisation) and **centralised inspection** with Network Firewall or appliances, where **appliance mode** keeps both directions of a flow in the same AZ.

Costs are per attachment-hour plus per GB processed, so heavy VPC-to-VPC flows may still justify direct peering. CIDRs must not overlap; manage them with VPC IPAM. For multi-Region, policy-driven networks, AWS Cloud WAN builds on the same ideas.
concepts.code:
TGW=$(aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --description core \
  --options DefaultRouteTableAssociation=disable,DefaultRouteTablePropagation=disable \
  --query TransitGateway.TransitGatewayId --output text)

ATT_PROD=$(aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-id "$TGW" \
  --vpc-id vpc-prod --subnet-ids subnet-tgw-a subnet-tgw-b \
  --query TransitGatewayVpcAttachment.TransitGatewayAttachmentId --output text)

RT_PROD=$(aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-route-table --transit-gateway-id "$TGW" \
  --query TransitGatewayRouteTable.TransitGatewayRouteTableId --output text)

# Prod looks up routes in RT_PROD, which learns only shared services
# (ATT_SHARED = the shared-services VPC attachment, created the same way)
aws ec2 associate-transit-gateway-route-table \
  --transit-gateway-route-table-id "$RT_PROD" --transit-gateway-attachment-id "$ATT_PROD"
aws ec2 enable-transit-gateway-route-table-propagation \
  --transit-gateway-route-table-id "$RT_PROD" --transit-gateway-attachment-id "$ATT_SHARED"

# The VPC side still needs a route to the TGW
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-prod-priv-a \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.0.0.0/8 --transit-gateway-id "$TGW"
takeaways: Peering is non-transitive; TGW is a transitive regional hub
Association picks an attachment's lookup table; propagation advertises its routes
Multiple TGW route tables give segmentation between environments
Share via RAM, avoid overlapping CIDRs, and watch per-GB processing costs
pitfalls: Forgetting the VPC subnet route to the TGW, so traffic never enters the hub even though TGW routes look right.

quiz.q: Prod and dev VPCs must both reach shared services but never each other. How?
options: One TGW route table with all attachments propagating
Separate route tables for prod and dev, each learning only shared-services routes
VPC peering between prod and dev
quiz.explain: Segmentation comes from associating prod and dev with different tables and controlling propagation.

quiz.q: VPC A peers with B, and B peers with C. Can A reach C through B?
options: Only if B has a NAT gateway
quiz.explain: Peering connections don't forward traffic between other peers; that's what Transit Gateway solves.

concepts.name: PrivateLink and interface endpoints
concepts.summary: Expose and consume services privately across VPCs and accounts with interface endpoints and NLB-backed endpoint services.
concepts.why: PrivateLink connects services without routing whole networks together, which sidesteps overlapping CIDRs and shrinks the attack surface.
concepts.body:
**AWS PrivateLink** provides private, one-directional connectivity to a *service* rather than to a network.

**Consuming AWS services**: an **interface VPC endpoint** for, say, `com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.sqs` creates an ENI with a private IP in each subnet you choose. With **private DNS** enabled, the normal hostname `sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com` resolves to those private IPs inside the VPC, so SDKs work unchanged and traffic never needs a NAT or internet gateway. Endpoints have security groups (allow 443 from your workloads) and **endpoint policies** that restrict which actions and resources can be used through them.

**Providing your own service**: put it behind a **Network Load Balancer** and create an **endpoint service**. Consumers in other VPCs or accounts create interface endpoints to its service name; you control which principals may connect and can require manual acceptance. Traffic is consumer-initiated only, the provider never sees the consumer's network, and overlapping CIDRs don't matter because nothing is routed between the VPCs. This is how most SaaS vendors offer private connectivity.

Trade-offs and details:

- Billed per endpoint per AZ-hour plus per GB; dozens of endpoints in many VPCs add up, so larger organisations centralise them in a shared VPC.
- Gateway endpoints remain the free option for S3 and DynamoDB within a VPC.
- Match AZs: a consumer endpoint can only use AZs where the provider's NLB has capacity, and AZ names differ per account, so compare AZ IDs.
- **VPC Lattice** offers an application-layer alternative for service-to-service traffic, with auth policies and HTTP routing.
concepts.code:
# Consumer: private access to SQS from isolated subnets
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --vpc-id vpc-app \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.sqs \
  --subnet-ids subnet-priv-a subnet-priv-b --security-group-ids sg-endpoints \
  --private-dns-enabled

# Provider: publish an NLB-fronted service
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint-service-configuration --acceptance-required \
  --network-load-balancer-arns "$NLB_ARN" \
  --query ServiceConfiguration.ServiceName --output text
# com.amazonaws.vpce.eu-west-1.vpce-svc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890
aws ec2 modify-vpc-endpoint-service-permissions --service-id vpce-svc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \
  --add-allowed-principals arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root

# Consumer account connects; provider accepts
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --vpc-id vpc-partner \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.vpce.eu-west-1.vpce-svc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \
  --subnet-ids subnet-x subnet-y --security-group-ids sg-x
aws ec2 accept-vpc-endpoint-connections --service-id vpce-svc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \
  --vpc-endpoint-ids vpce-0123456789abcdef0
takeaways: Interface endpoints are ENIs with private IPs; private DNS keeps hostnames unchanged
Endpoint services expose an NLB-fronted service to other accounts
Consumer-initiated and not routed, so overlapping CIDRs are fine
Costs are per endpoint-AZ-hour plus data; centralise when many VPCs need them
pitfalls: Enabling an interface endpoint without allowing 443 from workloads in the endpoint's security group.

quiz.q: A SaaS vendor's VPC uses the same 10.0.0.0/16 CIDR as yours. Which option still gives private connectivity?
quiz.explain: PrivateLink doesn't route between VPCs, so overlapping CIDRs are not a problem.

quiz.q: What lets SDK calls to sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com use an interface endpoint without code changes?
quiz.explain: Private DNS makes the public service hostname resolve to the endpoint's private IPs inside the VPC.

concepts.name: Throttling, quotas, retries and idempotency
concepts.summary: Build clients that survive AWS throttling and quotas: backoff with jitter, bounded retries and timeouts, idempotency tokens, eventual consistency.
concepts.why: At scale every AWS API pushes back, and naive retries turn a small throttle into a self-inflicted outage.
concepts.body:
Every AWS API is **rate limited**: call it too fast and requests are refused (throttled). Limits are usually token buckets per account, Region and operation; EC2 `Describe*` calls share buckets, for example. Throttles show up as `ThrottlingException`, `TooManyRequestsException`, `RequestLimitExceeded`, or HTTP 503 `SlowDown` from S3.

S3 scales per key prefix: thousands of requests per second per prefix, growing gradually. **Service Quotas** are separate: limits on resource counts and rates, either adjustable (request an increase before launch, and alarm on usage metrics) or fixed.

Retry well:

- **Exponential backoff with full jitter**: wait a random time between 0 and `min(cap, base * 2^attempt)` before each retry. Doubling gives a struggling service room; the randomness (**jitter**) stops many clients from retrying in the same waves.
- **Bound everything**: few attempts, connect and read timeouts below your caller's timeout, and retry at one layer only; retries stacked across layers multiply load.
- SDK **standard** mode adds a retry quota that stops retrying when most calls fail; **adaptive** mode adds client-side rate limiting.

**Idempotency** makes retries safe. Many create APIs accept an **idempotency token** (`ClientToken` on EC2 `RunInstances`, `ClientRequestToken` in CloudFormation and Secrets Manager): repeating a request with the same token returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate. Apply the same idea in your own APIs with idempotency keys.

**Eventual consistency** in control planes: a just-created resource may not be visible to `Describe` calls for a moment, and IAM changes take seconds to spread. Use waiters, and retry `NotFound` briefly after creates.

Finally, keep **control-plane** calls (create, modify) out of recovery paths; rely on **data-plane** operations and capacity provisioned in advance.
takeaways: Expect throttling; back off exponentially with full jitter
Bound retries and timeouts, and retry at one layer only
Use idempotency tokens so retried creates don't duplicate
Control planes are eventually consistent: use waiters and keep them out of recovery paths
pitfalls: Retrying in the SDK, the application and the load balancer at once, multiplying traffic during an incident.

quiz.q: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
options: To stop many clients retrying in synchronized waves
quiz.explain: Without jitter, throttled clients retry at the same moments and collide again.

quiz.q: A RunInstances call times out and you retry with the same ClientToken. What happens if the first call actually succeeded?
options: The call fails with a conflict
The original result is returned and no duplicate is launched
quiz.explain: Idempotency tokens make the retried request return the original outcome.

concepts.name: Multi-Region architectures and failover
concepts.summary: Replicate data across Regions, route users with Route 53 and recovery controls, and fail over (and back) without split brain.
concepts.why: For the strictest availability targets a Region itself is a failure domain, and getting multi-Region wrong adds more risk than it removes.
concepts.body:
Going multi-Region multiplies cost and complexity, so do it only when RTO/RPO or latency demand it. The hard part is **data**, because each store copies it differently:

- **S3 Cross-Region Replication**, with Replication Time Control for a 15-minute replication target.
- **DynamoDB global tables**: every Region accepts writes; copies are asynchronous by default, and if two Regions change the same item the last write wins. A multi-Region strong consistency mode exists for workloads that need it.
- **Aurora Global Database**: one primary Region and read-only secondaries fed from the storage layer, typically under a second behind. A **switchover** is planned and loses no data; a **failover** after a Regional outage promotes a secondary and may lose the last seconds of writes.
- Caches, search indexes and queues need their own story, often rebuild-on-failover.

**Traffic**: Route 53 latency or failover records with health checks, or Global Accelerator with fixed anycast IP addresses. For deliberate, reliable switching use **Route 53 Application Recovery Controller** routing controls, which work through a highly available data plane rather than control-plane changes during the incident.

Principles that separate working designs from slideware:

- **Static stability**: the standby Region already has the capacity, quotas, AMIs, images, secrets (multi-Region keys) and configuration it needs, all deployed from the same infrastructure-as-code pipeline.
- **Decide failover explicitly**: automatic flapping between Regions can cause **split brain**, two writers diverging. Many teams automate detection but keep a human decision to fail over.
- Plan **failback**, including re-synchronising the old primary.
- Practise with game days and deliberately injected faults (AWS FIS).
concepts.code:
# DynamoDB: add a replica Region to make a global table
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name orders \
  --replica-updates '[{"Create": {"RegionName": "eu-central-1"}}]'

# Aurora: turn an existing cluster into a Global Database with a DR secondary
aws rds create-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier orders-global \
  --source-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:eu-west-1:111122223333:cluster:orders
aws rds create-db-cluster --region eu-central-1 --db-cluster-identifier orders-dr \
  --engine aurora-postgresql --global-cluster-identifier orders-global \
  --db-subnet-group-name app-db --vpc-security-group-ids sg-db-dr

# Planned move, no data loss
aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier orders-global \
  --target-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:eu-central-1:111122223333:cluster:orders-dr

# Regional outage: promote the secondary, accepting possible loss of recent writes
aws rds failover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier orders-global \
  --target-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:eu-central-1:111122223333:cluster:orders-dr \
  --allow-data-loss
takeaways: Data replication is the hard part; know each store's lag and conflict model
Switchover is planned and lossless; failover after an outage can lose recent writes
Pre-provision everything in the standby Region (static stability)
Guard against split brain and plan failback; rehearse regularly
pitfalls: Relying on control-plane actions, such as creating resources or editing DNS, in the middle of a Regional outage.

quiz.q: Two Regions both accept writes to the same DynamoDB global table item at nearly the same time. What happens by default?
options: Last writer wins and replicas converge
quiz.explain: Default global tables are multi-active and resolve conflicts with last-writer-wins.

quiz.q: Why do many teams keep the final failover decision manual even with automated health checks?
options: Health checks can't detect Regional outages
To avoid flapping and split brain from false positives
quiz.explain: An automatic failover on a false positive can create two diverging primaries.
